I really enjoyed this game (PvE only), but there's a lot of hype and it isn't for everyone. If you're looking for a well-told and gripping story, characters you get attached to who develop through the game, and interesting quests, this IS NOT the game for that. If you're looking for a cool open world with beautiful scenery, minimal NPC interaction, a deep RPG system with lots of build flexibility, and super fun combat, this IS the game for that. You can adjust the difficulty by over/under leveling; I was probably a bit over-leveled most of the time because I explored a lot, so I thought it was hard, but not as hard as many other games I've played. There's enough to do that you can save the tough parts for when you're overpowered, or you could choose to never level up and go for a no-hit run. The Bad: Most of the quests and NPCs are boring, and some of the quests need to be completed before others for no obvious reason. This leads to some items being easily missed. The story itself is kind of interesting, but it isn't presented in a compelling way, so it's hard to care about the world or the people in it. This is compounded by the fact that there aren't really any towns, townsfolk, etc. to grow attached to. Finally, while for the most part the boss fights are awesome, there are one or two that are glitchy and/or tedious. The Good: The world is beautiful, and the locations are interesting and varied. The combat is wonderful, and the RPG systems are deep and flexible. There are lots of viable builds, weapons, and spells that can make gameplay feel very different. After the second main area, you can respec more or less freely. Exploring the overworld and various dungeons is fun and rewarding. Your mount can double jump and is a good boy. Overall, I loved this game, and it's one of my all-time favorites now. I would recommend it to anyone looking for a mechanically and aesthetically brilliant action RPG who doesn't care too much if the story and characters are a bit mediocre.

A very addictive and mostly fun game ... YET ... it is also a frustrating time-sink. This is a PvE-single-player-explore-and-conquer dream. But I don't recommend it. It is frustratingly difficult at times. The story is non-existent. There are no quest guides to help you navigate the open world. I am playing the game with a 12900k + 4090 yet it frequently stutters during combat, even though it's weirdly locked to 60 FPS. My 2017 7700k + 1080 Ti could do 4k60 so ... what gives? This game feels a lot like Elder Scrolls games: sure there's a main questline / goal but you can totally ignore it and just wander around and do stuff. I never finished Oblivion or Skyrim; I wandered around, leveled up, did some quest lines, joined some guilds, then got bored and stopped playing altogether. Elden Ring has been similar ... I'm 160+ hours in and have leveled a lot and explored but now feel fatigue & boredom. Since there's no story development, I don't feel any connection to the world and the characters in it ... why do I even care about becoming the Elden Lord and stopping the baddies in this world? Since there are no quest markers, I often find NPCs dead (as evidenced by them being a pile of lootable armor) having missed meeting them at the correct time. But, I usually just shrug at this because the game doesn't give me a reason to care. Will I come back to this at some point and play more? Absolutely. And, if you choose to buy this game, I'm sure you'll enjoy it at some level ... just understand what you're getting into.

Go check out Malcolm Reynolds on Youtube first of all, cool guy. So this game has a problem, a big one. The devs are trying to stomp out all cheating, so the coding community has double downed and created multiple ways to bypass EAC WHILE ONLINE. Welcome to the old DS3 days of getting crashed, and softbanned without knowing your inventory was edited. The issue isn't incredibly prevalent right now, but as a former CE coder for DS3 I can tell you quite easily where we are headed. Once the game drops in price, it'll be overran. A lot of people now are just using whatever edits they can get away with, and some people are even buying multiple copies to ban evade. So right now it's not a super invasive issue, but within a year it will be. The price drop will hit, hackers will buy up multiple copies, and the harassment will begin. Do you remember frame DCed? Do you remember the crashes so bad that you had to restart your PC? Do you remember being teleported into a room, with no way out, and all your bonfires disabled? We are heading that direction. It's inevitable no matter what they do with the AC, but now the devs are trying to ban anyone, and everyone who uses any sort of edit of any kind. I don't see harm in people editing their level for PvP, and I don't see issues with people creating new builds via CE editing (changing bullet values so you can use boss spells, or spells that are hidden within the code) A lot of this is really cool, and we even made a community in DS3 to prevent blackhats from ruining our fightclubs. We'd have an omega hacker defending the fight club, crashing anyone he detected as a blackhat. Now? Nobody wants to defend anymore, and you can still be force invaded at any time. There's no way to defend yourself unless you want to catch a ban. I personally ran countercheats to crash hackers if they messed with me. Now? Defending myself will net me a ban. Now let's talk about the game. This is by far the hardest "souls" game to be released, the threads complaining about everything after you reach the point of no return, are numerous. The ultra super special boss, even popular streamers are saying shes boring, and the only way to win is to remember her combos perfectly. No variation to that fight, if you try to get some space, rush combo, if you try to position, rush combo. It's just playing 100% defense and hoping you can land occasional hits. If she manages to hit you, she heals. So that's fun. Outside the last 4 or 5 bosses, the game is great. Once you hit that endgame it's like the Berlin wall, won't come down for some time. The majority of players I talk to are gated after or right before Fire Giant. The game RAMPS incredibly hard during that period, where a fully kitted, max level, max stat character can still be 2 shotted. How do you think those fights go for anyone around 140? The recommended level. It doesn't, seen too many people whine about difficulty, and quit. I personally agree, the late game ramps just a little too hard, and relies on mechanics that are just not fun. I'd rather play bloodborne, or DS3 any day. Most people who disagree with my opinion, also follow with "GIT GUD LOL BAD SCRUB" Yet, I'm not seeing as many as I did during DS3, maybe it's because that game was actually fair? Only 33% of players have beat that super hard boss that I was talking about early on, and 19% of players have even beat the game. Some people say that the last two bosses of the story, are harder than anything else. I personally think that the secret boss is the hardest boss I've ever beat legit. This is coming from someone who soloed the bloodborne DLC with no deaths from the bosses. Soloed all the souls games except this one, there must be something wrong here right? Food for thought. Not really worth 60$ for a game that you will probably quit near endgame.

The best souls game for me by far. I've played every single souls game since DS1 but this game takes the crown for me. The game is a souls like game but with a heavy emphasis on "open world", which IMO is amazing and there should be more of this. I'm a big enjoyer of these open world games so for me it was an easy S tier maybe even S+ with the DLC when it comes out. Most people who criticize this game are used to the classic souls like experience where you just follow a set guideline and stay on it, meanwhile this game throws that out of the water and lets you go anywhere you want whenever you want. I already beat the game once just rushing through it and even then it was extremely fun. The game has lots of replay ability and some people have even 10+ replays, every time you discover something new and different than your previous play-through. Right now I'm doing my 100% play-through, meaning I discover and do every single thing the game, get every single weapon, talisman, etc. I think this is the way to go in terms of playing the game and brings the most out of it, very fun game and definitely recommend it even for the somewhat steep $60.

This game is more or less like every other FromSoft game, for better and worse. There's really no reinventing of the wheel here aside from the open world. In some cases this works against and in favor of the player experience. The open world aspect is pretty fun, there's a lot of really picturesque things to see and screenshot worthy areas that are incredible first time around, but that's kind of where the benefits end. If that's a huge deal to you, you'll love it. For everything else, it's kind of a step in the opposite direction. Quests follow the standard FromSoft 'we won't tell you shit about what you're supposed to do, who to find, who to kill, figure it out on your own.' This approach is serviceable in their other games because of their size but is terrible in a game this large. It might give players an excuse for multiple NG+, but when you spent upwards of 150 hours and there are quests you still need to look up online because you have no idea what random shit ends them or where to go, and this is every quest, it becomes a problem. It's more of a problem when, in FromSoft fashion, much of the lore is hidden behind items, subtle interactions that may or may not have branching paths (again, some of which end quests entirely). To me, this is just not enjoyable. I don't mind having to find items to learn the lore, but the content is not easily accessible and becomes an irritation. The open world also makes this game the easiest to over level on, either accidentally or on purpose. I ended up clearing Caelid after Stormveil Castle because of the lack of direction and trivialized much of the game after and I feel like I lost out on a lot of first time experiences because of it when I went back to lower level areas. The PvP is also in a god awful state. The balancing is more or less OK after so many iterations of patches, but the lag is terrible. People walking through your spells and attacks, frames in animations being skipped, a hit registering and dealing no damage (I found this one out using Gargoyle's Blackblade), or being plus frames in a situation and the lag makes you lose out -- a colossal weapon beating out a rapier in speed for instance. The camera and lock-on are also some of the biggest messes I've seen since Red Ninja, the platforming is still mostly unusable and should be scrapped entirely. It's not all bad though. Despite some bosses having broken hurt boxes, they're mostly well designed and challenging. The characters themselves, once you're actually able to access their lore, have some of the most compelling stories in any FromSoft game. This is easily FromSoft at their best if we ignore Sekiro, which was a masterpiece, and makes it hard to really look at any earlier Souls games without wondering why you wouldn't just play this instead. You should probably get it if these types of games interest you, but there are some pretty big glaring issues and some subjective things you might not enjoy. I still can't get over the experience systems in these games, but I accept it when I play them.

I'll start off by saying I've been enjoying Dark Souls since DS1. Fromsoft makes some excellent games and this game is good, but my negative review comes from a few things I don't enjoy and I don't think the series needed. We didn't need a open world. It's as wide as an ocean and shallow as a puddle. I prefer the old linear experience that Dark Souls has always provided. I also stand that I wish we could get back to the inter connectivity that DS1 demonstrated so excellently. I become incredibly disappointed when I clear a side dungeon only to fight a boss I previously killed. It ruins the excitement of finding something new only to experience something old. The reuse of bosses in this game kills the experience for me. The boss design is also another factor in my review. I've always been a hyper aggressive player. I look for openings in between attacks while still being able to roll dodge as well. I'm aggressive and hate playing passive. I enjoy optimizing and looking for zero downtime if possible. That said, these bosses will string together a Marvel Vs Capcom string for 30 seconds and I'm just stuck standing away and looking at the boss like I'm stupid. After that string they have almost zero downtime and begin to run the string once again. It's not fun to constantly be dodging for 30+ seconds only to maybe hit once or twice. In closing, we sacrificed quality for quantity. The game has the highest highs of the series followed by devastatingly low lows that ruin it for me.

I have been playing FROM Software games since DS1 came out on the 360. I have tried to like these games over and over. I have played DS1 from many different angles and many different classes, but have never seen the appeal. To me, playing these games just feels like training yourself to be really good at executing a half-baked feedback loop process with extremely broken tools, and Elden Ring is no exception. Not only does this game exemplify everything wrong with the design of FROM games, but it doesn't even do it in an original or groundbreaking way like lots of people would have you believe. The combat is almost exactly like DS1, and the bosses are an odd hybrid of styles and presentation from Souls, Bloodborne, and Sekiro. The open world is lifeless and dull, and the game dumps needlessly obtuse exposition with no explanation of other parts of the lore or why you as the player should care. It's just "go on a great quest, oh chosen Undead!" Yeah, I haven't seen that anywhere else... except it's the premise for every FROM game since Dark Souls. Truly I am absolutely baffled as to how this game won any awards, much less Game of the Year. If you want a video game that you can install, have fun with, and put down until you wanna play again, this is NOT the game for you. If you like games where you have to sink an extreme amount of time and research into the world's lore, the broken combat system, and the general obtuse and bloated design of the game in hopes that you MIGHT be capable of squeezing out even the smallest crumbs of fun from it, then be my guest here. Hopefully I can at least get a refund so I can say I spent my money on a game I will actually play instead of a game that I boot up, play for 5 minutes, be reminded why I didn't buy at launch, die due to broken hit detection, and turn off again for 3 or 4 more weeks. Maybe I'm old school, but I think video games should be fun right out of the box. Part of the reason I love PC gaming specifically is because there is so much variety to be had in terms of game experiences, whether in terms of "pick up and play" or "big time sink" type games like this one. And that is definitely not to say that all games that require you to put time and research into them are bad; some of my favorite games are Stalker, Silent Hill, and Disco Elysium, all games that require you to retain and put effort into the world and just being in the game. But this game, to me, epitomizes the soulless AAA product machine that gaming has become. "Explore the open world!" Why? Is there anything worth seeing there? Is there a good story? Or does everything in this game ultimately serve as just fluff in between hours of grinding that you're expected to just enjoy without any clear motivation as to why you should be enjoying it? And even then, when the story DOES show up, it's the exact same pseudo-verbose fake Tolkien crap FROM has been spoon-feeding their blood-loyal fans since Dark Souls. Seriously, if you want to waste your time "getting gud" at a broken ass game, at least do it with Bloodborne. You'd be doing yourself a service to save up the money to buy a PS4 just to buy Bloodborne over playing this one. I'm probably SOL on getting a refund, so if you see I have higher hours now than when I wrote this review, it is because I am simply trying to complete the game to get my money's worth and uninstall it so I can go back to playing something else.

SCORE: 8/10 Elden Ring initially gripped me in a way few other games have. The starting area of Limgrave is superbly designed, offering a significant amount of enemy variety, enticing landscapes and plenty to explore. The sense of awe and wonder is strong, perhaps unrivalled among open world games. The areas that immediately follow it maintain a high level of quality, even if not quite high as the opening area. The repetition of the caves, catacombs, etc. was starting to wear a little thin, the amount of reused bosses was becoming more noticeable and my frustration at how little of the loot I was finding was relevant to my build was growing, but the first fifty hours or so were nevertheless extremely engaging. Unfortunately, there is a point in the game at which those minor flaws start to become major ones. The enemy variety is extremely front-loaded, leading to dozens of hours of playtime in the latter half of the game fighting almost nothing but reused enemies. Exploration became unrewarding when it began to dawn on me just how few of the things I was finding I even considered using. The repetitive open world filler content had long worn out its welcome. The more I played, the more I began to think this is not some new, innovative approach to open world design as many people claim. If, for example, clearing out an enemy camp in an Assassin's Creed game is considered a bad example of content to put in an open world, I don't see how clearing out a copy-paste catacomb, fighting a boss I've seen several times before at the end of it and opening a chest to get a weapon I'll never use is much of an improvement. The presentation of this content, choosing not to mark it on the map beforehand and put a check mark next to it when you're done, is welcome. But the standard of the actual content itself once you find it is not any better than what other open world games have to offer. As with many other open world games, I think Elden Ring would be better if it showed more restraint. There is simply just not enough interesting content to fill its huge world. It's a game with many memorable moments, but almost all of those came in the first half of the ninety-five hours I spent playing it.

I don't like Souls games. I suck at Souls games. Bounce right off 'em. I didn't even like THIS game at first; it spits you into a hostile world, points you vaguely in a direction likely to get you killed and tells you to figure it out. That isn't immediately fun. But then I started experiencing things I'd never associated with Souls before: A huge variety of weapons, with fighting styles and animations to match. Enormous freedom to build your character, including impressive magic systems (I'd always just associated Souls with fairly dry sword-and-shield combat). Exploration is always rewarding, with oodles of actually-useful, unique goodies to be found in the world's various nooks and crannies. A decent roster of summons to help with tough encounters, and many other tools to approach challenges. And while it does punish you in a way other games don't, you stop minding after a while and are never stuck in one spot, even at an important story boss. The art direction is superb, capturing both brightness and ominous dark. The game is so freeform that your way through it might be alien to another player, yet it feels rich and complete in a way that is rare in the era of microtransactions, battle passes etc. Elden Ring refreshingly has none of that. Cons? The game needed a journal. Quests can break if you make the wrong bit of progress at the wrong time, and you'll frequently hit a roadblock because you haven't poked the right illusory wall in the right dungeon out of a hundred or so or didn't talk to that one guy in that backwater ruin enough times. This isn't a dealbreaker; most of the fun is emergent and I actually felt more involved by starting up a pen-and-paper journal to track stuff. The lore is good, and creatively imparted, but it exists to serve the gameplay and build the immediate world, so don't go in expecting depth on the level of Elder Scrolls, Mass Effect, Horizon, etc. (Sorry Souls fans, I know this is a point of pride.) The tone is also relentlessly depressing. The game world is pretty much post-apocalyptic, and outside a handful of NPCs the only people are maddened or otherwise hostile. Don't get attached to any of the characters you meet because there are almost no happy endings for any of them. I had to remind myself to come up for air occasionally to avoid it affecting my IRL mood. Performance isn't perfect even a year post-launch, with some unusual frame drops here and there, but it still ran okay on my old laptop as well as my stronger desktop. KBM controls are atrocious; you’ll want a controller. None of this brings Elden Ring down. It's a deeply involving experience that has dominated two months of my life, and I don't regret it. It won't hold your and through any part of it I still don't know if these games are really my thing, but Elden Ring will stick with me for a long time for a lot of good reasons. I can think of several different builds and weapon classes I want to go back and try, and there are a couple of areas and major bosses I haven't even touched yet, never mind the other endings. Easy 9/10.

Elden Ring is a Challenging yet rewarding experience as you traverse through large open world landscapes permeating with enemies and bosses of all different shapes, sizes and attack styles. The game (much like the soulsbourne series in general) is an excellent personification of life itself. Focusing on a format where through your many struggles and setbacks, if you learn from your mistakes and persevere, you will prevail. Their are multiple different classes to choose that allow you to play the game how you see fit, so their is no right or wrong way to play and is purely up to player on how best to approach a situation and to embrace or strategise your strengths and weaknesses. The game is also very well polished (a rarity in modern gaming) with clear forethought in its design, very minimal bugs were present in my play through and the combat seems very well balanced. The story is conveyed mostly through lore, requiring the player to research the details of the characters and they're history, ambitions & goals to create a better understand of the world. Some may be disappointed in its lack of presence but personally this works in favour of the game, as its there if you are interested to learn, and if you're not then just carry on and it won't matter (Radahn has the best backstory btw). needless to say I adore Elden Ring and look forward to seeing more from Fromsoftware :) tl;dr Overall Elden Ring is easily the best way to get into the Soulsbourne series of games, its challenging yet rewarding, has fairly balanced combat, the open world is mesmerising, extensive lore. their is lots to love about this game 10/10 GOTY for 2022

ELDEN RING I wanted to be objective on this review so I left it for some while and waited for my excitement to go down. Fromsoftware and their games are my favourites. I love Souls-Borne series the most of all games. I started with Dark Souls 2 and after it played through Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, Sekiro. DS1 and Demon Souls I saw on the live stream. Then I played an absurd amount of souls-like games from other studios or indie developers, for example: Surge 1+2, Hellpoint, Lords of the Fallen, Nioh 1+2, Ashen, Mortal Shell, Salt and Sanctuary, Code Vein, Thymesia, Death's Gambit etc. The point is I love the souls like formula in the games and all these games that I mentioned are great but I wanted something fresh, because all of these game follows the same pattern. When Elden Ring was first announced I thought of it as no big deal, but man was I wrong. Elden Ring took the souls formula and pushed it to another level - open world. It could sound terrifying but it isn't, trust me. The masters from Fromsoftware did absolutely amazing job in implementing all that we like into an open world. The world is full of activities, enemies, bosses, items (every one item except consumables has its own specific place), NPCs and stories and full of amazing lore that we love. The game challenges you at every corner and I thought not even once that I'm bored. Worlds on Ubisoft "checklist" basis are nothing compared to the world of Elden Ring. Build variety is as amazing, maybe better than in Dark Souls. Main dungeons are sweet and complex locations like in the previous games. Side dungeons are okey, sometimes they look similar to each other, but it depend on "biome" in which you currently are. There are lot of secret tombs and theres questline for witch Ranni, that opens a whole area of the map that you cannot find otherway. Skills, spells, weapons feel epic and adds a lot of flavour to your playthrough. It's a fresh wind for souls games and I hope the coming DLC would be even better than the main storyline. Pros and cons: + Amazing open world + It feels like Dark Souls but better + Graphics are slightly better but nothing big, so I felt like home from the beggining + Epic bosses, even better than in previous games (I mean main bosses) + Great lore and exploration - It's not ideal for a newbies to souls games For me Elden Ring is 10/10 game, that will have a place in my heart for eternity.

My gripes with this game run deep. Starting with the console style gaming. I play PC for a reason... keyboard and mouse primarily. Being forced to play where a controller design is intended is very annoying to me. The game world is vast, and beautiful, and fun to explore. Enemies look interesting. The atmosphere is great. Those are the only pluses I would attribute to Elden Ring. Combat ruins the game however, in my opinion. The camera control is lousy and locked targets will switch mid-combat to targets you are not even engaged with. It is always fun fighting an enemy directly in front of you and having the camera rotate 180 degrees because it randomly locks some enemy behind you. At that point, you are still facing and fighting the front enemy but with the camera spinning, missing all your attacks, and not even knowing which way is up or down after the vertigo the game puts you through. Every fight is painful and it is not because of how the enemy fights most of the time, but rather, it is because of how lousy the controls are with keyboard and mouse. I also believe in fair combat for games, with a decent AI. Elden Ring is anything but this. Once you start going into boss fights, all they do is stay on you with either their 10x speed movement, or jump onto you from the other side of the arena. Your character is very sluggish in comparison. Not only is enemy boss movement at super speed, but they do not have status bars themselves, other than HP, so they spam boss abilities. To me, I find it to be a cheaty and lousy AI. It's not really about tactics but more about learning the rotations and timings. The AI is just not good. A lot of people say "git gud" but I think that should be directed at these companies for not developing any kind of decent AI in these games and just going with the same old worn-out model every single time. This game feels like a step backwards. Instead of meaningful combat, this game is all about timing that dodge roll. I find it sad that games have not progressed beyond parkour and the dodge roll. >.>

It's been two and a half months now since I 100%'ed this game. I haven't had the urge to go back to it a single time since. I didn't hate the time I spent with it, but I wouldn't say I enjoyed it either. I had never played a FromSoftware game before – whenever I saw someone play one of their Souls-games I thought "Wow that looks absolutely horrible and about as fun as going to the dentist." And I didn't necessarily mean the difficulty (and more specifically the way in which they are "difficult"), but also the aesthetics and how the movement and physics looked like. But, given the absolutely insane hype levels for Elden Ring I decided to finally give one of them a shot. Unfortunately my intuition was correct: The movement does feel like you're controlling a semi truck on molasses. It just does not *feel* fun to do anything in this game, be it running around or fighting. I'm not talking about the way heavy vs. light loadouts feel, the very foundations of movement and physics in this game just don't appeal to me. Of course as a Souls-beginner it also took some getting used to, but that happened fairly quickly. I didn't have any trouble with it, but it's not something that would draw me to the game – which is problematic, considering that movement makes up most of the gameplay. The other part, the aesthetics, also mostly didn't click for me just as I expected. Don't get me wrong, I can appreciate that the art direction in this game is very well done. (I do think that it's a tad bit overhyped, though – the game looks good, but it doesn't look great.) But with very few exceptions it is all just pain and despair, mud and dirt, darkness and gloom. There's not enough contrast between areas that are some variation of "big end of the world mood" and more light-hearted areas. I understand that this makes sense from a story perspective, but it's just not something I enjoy very much. Why would I want to spend 100+ hours in this utterly depressing hellscape, with no respite to make it all worth it? Speaking of story… well. It certainly has some GRRM aspects to it, but not so much the good ones that gave us amazing stories well over a decade ago, but the ones that just drip feed the idea of something bigger and better still to come, pinky promise, anytime now! If you're lucky enough to even stumble upon some story, it's usually confusing and feels irrelevant/disconnected. I hate modern Ubisoft open world games as much as anyone else, but Elden Ring absolutely does not even come close to do this right in the way that Breath of the Wild did. The fact that most players will go to a Wiki to be able to figure out how to finish (or even find and begin…) quest lines is a scathing indictment of how badly the game fails at telling its stories. The "async coop" did not click with me either. The ghosts of other players pretty much never revealed anything of interest to me. At best they could be ignored, at worst they were a distraction. Far worse are the hints, which gives a pretty good insight into the headspace of the fan base of this game. "try finger but hole" is their idea of peak comedy, and everyone falls over themselves making this same joke for the billionth time. More serious ones like "enemy/treasure ahead" are worthless as well, because you can never know if it is a troll or not. So you do check any nooks and crannies anyway – and there's nothing wrong with a game wanting you to do so, but what's the point of these hints then. Finally, the difficulty. Yeah, it's pretty hard if you don't farm XP and overlevel yourself. The game does an okay job of being a difficult game. Considering that it's a fairly complex 3D open world game, you can't expect great loading times after you die, but the gameplay also isn't designed for dying as often and freely as for example something like Celeste – which lets you continue playing after death within milliseconds. There's a couple of spots that are just infuriating, though, mostly to do with elevators. Site of grace next to the elevator, you ride it up and there's an area where you most likely will die a whole bunch of times before getting through. Every damn time after dying and respawning at the site of grace you not only have to ride back up – you first have to call the elevator back down because it is still above from your earlier ride. Of course that is logical and "correct", but that doesn't make it any less annoying. Resetting an elevator next to a site of grace to be on your level upon respawning would have been such an obvious QoL improvement, but Elden Ring does not give you any of those. And hardcore fans will defend that as realism, or a counter to the oh so horrible hand-holding that games do these days. But that's bs. Little annoyances like that don't make a game harder or "more real", they just make it more annoying. It's these kinds of things that make me think that Elden Ring was rushed out in the end, and I'm genuinely baffled by the praise it gets for supposedly being "one of the good ones" when compared to other AAA games and their need for day one patches. I didn't _mind_ the stuttering issues the game still has on PC, but they haven't even been fixed. I had _a ton_ of bugs and glitches and some crashes even. Nothing too bad or unexpected for a game of this scale, but Elden Ring is not some magic outlier here that does things much better or differently than other good AAA games, of which there is still plenty. So, do I recommend this game? No, I personally do not. If your taste in games is like mine, you won't enjoy it very much. I don't regret my time with it, because now I know definitively that Souls-games just aren't for me. But that thumbs-down is not meant to say that it's a bad game, despite all my criticisms above. A lot of them are very subjective, and the ones that I'd say are a bit more objective aren't dragging the game down too much. I can absolutely understand why people love this game, but unfortunately I didn't.

I will start off with, the game is fun and it is worth playing if you are new to the Souls series, or you suck at the Dark Souls games.. but... I don't get it.Id rather go back and play Dark Souls 3 personally.. I have easily several Hundred hours in DS1. well over 2000 in DS2 and at least the same amount in DS3. I don't get it. Elden Ring is not that great. After nearly 200h I can confidently say, Dark Souls was Better. The game is clearly made for Casuals, and the combat is kind of Braindead easy when you aren't being cheap shotted by a Boss with a mechanic that is unavoidable. Like, a lot of enemies will attack you as you are recovering from a Knockdown, hitting you BEFORE the animation even ends of you standing up, making you unable to avoid it. and that is the only thing you need to learn.. once you learn how to avoid the cheap shots.. the game becomes trivial. In the Souls Series, there were virtually no Cheap shots.. this game is littered with them, giving it Artificial difficulty. These things make it Seam difficult, but its really not. 9/10 Bosses in this game I can literally just sit there and Charged-Heavy the Boss to death with Caesti, no need to Dodge or avoid at all. Even with my Insane Regen build in past games, I never could do this. I get up to over 1000 AR with FISTS. FISTS! I can get a Guaranteed 3 hit combo off on another Player that deals a total of 3k damage, before Defenses.. even after defenses, most people are Dead after that... they Ruined Poise. While it is nice to have DS 1 and 2 Passive Poise back, even at Max Poise you can only survie 2 swings from a Longsword or equivalent. Anything Bigger still 1 tap staggers. If you just spec for Jumping Attacks, congrats! you beat the game. The Open World is nice, but it really doesn't offer much after the 1st playthrough. in the 1st Play through, the open world is fun and exciting. in the NG+x Playthroughs, its tedious and actually annoying to have to constantly navigate. 80% of this game is not mandatory to get to the next playthrough, as opposed to the Souls games, where it was the exact opposite. It is an interesting take, but since 80% of the game is just useless past the 1st playthrough, whats the point? You will get through NG+ in like 30 mins.. Its really not all that. The Ashes of War system is amazing and opens a lot of Options. Maybe in the future we get another game that gives us the option for actual Skills instead. If you don't want to go Punch enemies for 1k damage at level 70 and up, just go mage... you can nuke anything from Players to Bosses as a mage and they cannot do anything about it. Dont get me wrong, the Game is fun.. its just nowhere near as good as any of the People here want you to believe. there are Detrimental bugs that will piss you off in PvP, like a Bug to increase Rivers of Bloods Phantom reach by like 100x. And its damage doubles as well. Considerable amount of hackers are also still existing in the game. all in all, this is a perfect game for the Dark Souls Novice, and the Casuals that don't feel ready to enter the Tryhard community of the actual Souls games. but be prepared to know that most people are actually rather casual in this game, especially in PvP.. even in the Arenas, most ppl seem rather casual :/ RIP Dark Souls PvP standards

Tato hra je totální master piece Elden ring byla má první hra od vývojářského studia From Software a musím říct, že na mě studio udělalo obrovský dojem a hry od něj budu hrát i nadále. Ale co podle mě Elden Ring udělalo natolik úžasným? World: Postupné objevování světa je skvělé a až na výjimky se už od začátku můžeme dostat kamkoliv, což ve hrách vždy rád vidím, ale v Elden Ringu mě to potěšilo ještě více svojí různorodostí, až už travnatý a hornatý Lim Grave, pustý a děsivý Caelid, jezernatá Liurnia či jednoduše nádherná Siofra. Všechno to jsou opravdu krásně vybudované a obsahem narvané lokace ,u kterých se vám oči ani prsty nudit nebudou. Každá nabízí své unikátní nepřátele i atmosféru, která by se dala krájet. Jak rád bych opět zažil ten pocit co jsem měl při prvním spuštění. Ten pocit po touze objevovat a prozkoumat ten svět, který se předemnou právě otevřel do posledního koutku. A že má co nabídnout. I po spuštění NG+ se mi podařilo najít lokace o jejichž existenci jsem do teď neměl ani páru. K lokacím mám jen jednu jedinou výtku a to směrem k Weeping Peninsula, která toho dle mého nemá zas tolik co nabídnout, ale zase nechci říkat, že by se jednalo o něco špatného. Gameplay: Postava je krásně responzivní, reaguje přesně jak klikám a ani jednou se mi nestalo, že by opravdu dělal něco co sem nechtěl. U každého špatného rollu jsem věděl, že je to má chyba, stejně tak u každého pádu při platformové pasáži. Možná ovládání Torrenta je trochu prkené. Ovládání v soubojích je jednoduché na pochopení, příjemné a na ovládání. Ještě bych chtěl vypíchnout jak hra přistupuje k questům. Žádně question marky, které mi ukazují kam mám jít. Nic takového v Elden Ringu nenajdete. Sice možná některé questy budete procházet dle návodů na Wiki/YTB, ale to mi vůbec nevadilo. Naopak mě to těšilo tím jak hra není zbytečně zahlcená a není tam nic zbytečně navíc. Dále bych chtěl zmínit summons, kterých je ve hře opravdu dost. Postupem času odemykáte lepší. Summons můžete získat u traderů nebo z bossů. Které si pak vylepšujete stejně jako zbraně. Příběh: Osobně bych řekl, že studiem loru jsem strávil ještě víc času než na hře samotné. Propracovaná historie a malinkaté detaily, které ho doplňují, mě uchvátili více jak jakákoliv fantasy kniha či film co jsem kdy viděl. George Raymond Richard Martin odvedl při tvorbě tohoto světa naprosto fenomenální práci. Dobrá práce Georgi Finální verdikt: I přes to, že bych o Elden Ringu byl schopen mluvit dlouhé hodiny, udělám to jak stručně jen můžu: 11/10 +příběh/Lore +mechanika hry +prostředí +grafika +soundtracks ... This is legit the BIGGEST open world game I have ever played in my life. The sheer detailing of every region be it the art direction , enemy variety , level design , ambience & music is pure exquisite craftmanship from the developers. Despite the open world design & approach borrowing it's idea from ZELDA , Elden Ring absolutely takes it to another level making it an experience unlike any other game I have played. The game is bigger than anybody can fathom. At times it could be quite overwhelming to keep track of the regions you have discovered, the NPC interactions and the constant breaking of questlines but it's quite unique on how the game doesn't dump details at your face and rather rewards you for exploration and discovery with it's rich and mysterious lore. I also think this is by far the most accessible FROM SOFTWARE game mainly because of the amount of choices you are left with to approach the game. The game play and combat though is detailed & vast doesn't necessarily have the learning curve complexity of their PREVIOUS game SEKIRO. Some of the biggest issues I had with the game are the poor optimisation for PC performance despite a locked 60 fps even in my 3060 GPU. Most of the Dragon battles I faced had extreme stuttering in terms of performance. Also there are some questionable design choices in the UI , for instance every time the game has a popup window in the middle of a battle when I resummon Torrent after he is dead. I get the need of it in the initial stages of the game but why does it continue till the very end. It's very much distracting and can quite lead you to your death at times. At least they should have included an option to turn it off in the settings. Also for a game with it's absolutely incredible number of bosses , the biggest enemy you will ever face is going to be the CAMERA. As the POPULAR saying goes : " YOU CAN ESCAPE THE BOSSES , BUT NEVER THE CAMERA " 9/10 - HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

In Tetris, players must arrange falling shapes called tetrominoes in a way that creates horizontal lines without any gaps. As the game progresses, the tetrominoes fall faster and the player must think and move quickly in order to keep up. One of the great things about Tetris is that it is very easy to learn, but difficult to master. This means that players of all skill levels can enjoy the game, but there is always room for improvement and challenges for those who want to push themselves. Tetris is also a very social game, with many different variations available on Steam that allow players to compete against each other online, either cooperatively or in head-to-head matches. These variations can add an extra layer of fun and challenge to the game, as players must compete against others to see who can score the highest.

Elden Ring was my introduction to the Souls series of games-- and I think it might also be my stopping point. I had not played any Dark Souls games prior to this point, and the style of 3D combat was brand new to me at the outset. I was not foreign to difficult games, but most of the souls-like games I'd gotten good at by this point were 2D platformers and metroidvanias! Making the adjustment to camera controls was a learning curve and not being able to see everything at once tended to be a bit frustrating (at least at the start). That said, I knew the internet was an essential resource for the souls genre and a few beginners-guides later I was adapting to the game's language with relative ease. If this is your entry point, please, do yourself a favor and make a few google searches on easy class types and beginner's guides! You'll save yourself an immense amount of headache in the future. Once I was able to adapt to the style of gameplay, the world really opened up for me. I was BLOWN AWAY by the scale of the game-world and it's (relative) depth and detail. I found myself repeatedly enamored, shocked, and awed by the amount of impressive locations! This game does something that I genuinely appreciate: it is not afraid for you to not see all of it's content. Games like those produced by Ubisoft and others are determined to scatter a myriad of location markers and it takes all of the fun out of exploration (especially when said locations are copy-paste activities). But even a game world like Elden Ring's cannot avoid the curse of padding in some areas: particularly, the repeated cave dungeons and ruins started to become much less and less exciting. Running into them and trying to clear them out for items became a chore when I'd gotten through the brunt of the game's world but they're a necessity for progression due to the items they contain. That said, I think that it's much less atrocious in a game like Elden Ring and the world makes up for it in many ways; It's time I told you about my eclectic approach to discovery within this game's world. When I set out from the start, I ended up receiving a single map for the start of the game. The remaining game world was covered in unmarked brown spotted with clouds. A tiny neuron (or demon, depending on how you look at it) ignited and told me that I now NEEDED the full map of the game. This became my primary desire in the game moving forward: fill the map. Before I wanted to explore anything thoroughly, I would have to get the whole map. For games like Breath of the Wild, I was able to do this exact strategy and had a great time doing so. For Elden Ring, however, this would prove a unique challenge. Many areas of the game require items, boss completion, and a good deal of exploration to find ways to access. I took to the challenge and immediately began pushing in all directions to see how far I could go with very little upgrades and levels. To spare you the details of my entire journey (spoilers) this was incredibly difficult, but I managed to pull it off. I made it to the final mapped area of the game and had completed the set! From here, I began to explore the world more thoroughly and found it a great joy to go back to starting areas with my big boy items and absolutely cheese earlier challenges in the game. I made discoveries, I beat bosses, I played the game and had a lot of fun doing so: but it was around here that I discovered what I'd been enjoying most about the game and why that was about to change. You see, I was getting almost all of my enjoyment out of exploration. Once I'd managed to do almost all of that (I am currently located in the endgame areas having explored almost all of the world prior but only haven beaten about half the major bosses) my enjoyment of the game was severely drying up. If I'm being honest, I am not a huge fan of the combat in this game. Do NOT get me wrong, it is a superbly designed system which no doubt has been refined over the course of the Souls series, it provides a HUGE amount of strategic options (which I enjoyed making the most of as a Bleed-Build Warrior), and is accessible for a pretty wide range of skill levels, but it just wasn't my cup of tea. Like I mentioned earlier, the 3D environment makes it difficult for me to get a full picture of what's going on sometimes. The way the world is set up, enemies and bosses either tend to be really easy or stupidly difficult. I hate the four century wind-ups and waiting periods on some bosses, and while there were highlights, I would often give up direct approaches and trying to be good at dodging (as a melee build) and would eventually resort to either over-leveling, cheesing with summons, or any alternative strategy that would get me PAST the boss-fight and onto the cool new areas to explore. To put it more succinctly, once there was little left to explore, the core gameplay of Elden Ring didn't really entice me. I think it's a fantastic game that will stick out in my mind for a long time to come, but it has given me the impression that this was the only game in the Souls series that's going to appeal to me. That said, I HIGHLY recommend anybody interested in this game give it a go, as my experience will likely not resemble yours. I recommend you take your time with it and if you get stuck, don't be afraid to look up some help! I heard someone describe this game as "the dream game of 90's RPG developers" and I agree. 9.0/10.

That lore is still there, so don't get that crossed. The second huge improvement is that there's real platforming to do, though it only plays out in fights or boss battles some of the time. Most combat isn't much different than in the Souls titles, however, we've a dedicated jump button, ash summons, and several other tools at play we didn't in those other games. Would go on, but I'm pretty sure most people already know what to expect of a Souls-like game. My only word of warning is that this isn't Dark Souls. It's much easier if you wanna make it easier. It's also much harder if you wanna make it harder. By which I mean Elden Ring is really Dark Souls with options. A lot of different options to every fight and choice you make in game just about. The PC version at this point in time is the best place to play Elden Ring in my opinion. Runs very smoothly. That said, I'm writing this at 200+ hours and leaving only the last boss to beat. Elden Ring is marketed as an Open-World RPG that doesn't focus on it's open nature, instead pretending to be Dark Souls 4 (with too much space). Enemies frequently do too much damage per hit, meaning that players should either go all-in on HP or not bother with the stat (focus on evading instead). This game still punishes casters (as DS3 did: no FP-regen, staggering stat sinks required, sacrifice healing for FP flasks, etc.) while getting rid of weapon durability (infinite melee). FromSoft is clearly too heavily invested in making a "harder" game (difficulty is always subjective) and failed to flesh out key details of this title. The questlines are convoluted and offer no guidance, even Majora's Mask (2000) included an in-game utility to track NPCs. The worst part for me was finding out after refund-eligibility expired that the game didn't live up to its hype and the first real boss can easily be more than 2 hours in. Now I'm stuck fighting a game I should be enjoying instead. C'est la vie!

Eighty-ish hours and one trophy later, five takeaways from The Lands Between™: * The game's hardware requirements are correct: if you want to play Elden Ring at a consistent 1080p60, your CPU needs at least 6 cores and 12 threads. Never mind the main storyline, the true final boss is realizing that lowering the display resolution and graphics quality to 720p/Low won't get you a stable 60fps on an otherwise-serviceable quad-core CPU. If you don't have a hexacore CPU, see if your graphics software can lock the frame rate to 30; I found a steady 30fps to be a better visual experience than a stuttery ~45fps. * After a single, pseudo-100% clear spanning several weeks, speedrunning this twice for the other ending achievements was a breath of fresh air. * Vigor and armor can prevent being one-shot in combat, but nothing can prevent getting one-shot by fall damage. This rule applies to your enemies, too. * In a world where 'RTFM' is sage advice, if a game isn't going to explicitly tell you what's going on, never be ashamed to do your own research. It's always easier to search for information out-of-game than to search for your lost runes in-game. * Whoever made the final call on the HUD only displaying piecewise elements that were recently used without flickering or cluttering up the screen deserves high praise. Conversely, whoever made the final call on putting a boss directly in a pile of scarlet rot *more than once* needs to update their resume. * Bonus 6th takeaway: Malenia's a bully, but Waterfowl Dance is the only truly threatening aspect of her kit. Try complaining less and getting better at the game. Or you can equip Blasphemous Blade/Magma Wyrm Scalesword and press L2 after dodging, that works too.

Before starting the actual review, huge thanks to [b]director: Hidetaka Miyazaki[/b], [b]writer: George R. R. Martin[/b] and last but not least the [b]development team: FromSoftware[/b] for creating this beautiful and still "git gud" challenging video game for us to enjoy. Also congratulation for winning the [b]The Game Awards 2022 - Game of the Year[/b] and the [b]Steam Awards 2022 - Game of the Year[/b] trophies at least (on top of the bunch of other awards). TL;DR If you have liked the previous Dark Souls games or looking for real challenge from a action RPG genre, you just don't have any excuses for NOT to playing the [b]ELDEN RING[/b]. [b][u]It's that awesome and worth of every single coin you put into it.[/u][/b] For those who haven't tried out any of previous Dark Souls related games, I really recommend you to give it a try. Like previous games Elden Ring gives you life lessons of not giving up when you face the impossible obstacle, there is always solution to get pass that, even if it means making decisions that are not easy. Started playing with Intel i7-8700K & RTX 3080 -> a bit over middle way through upgraded to AMD 7600X & RTX 3080. This review is written in POV of character with following setup (can contain spoilers); [spoiler]Magic caster (lvl 165 50,50,30,13,13,70,8,10), no summons & spirit/war ashes used, no parrying, no great runes activated, no PVP, Malenia and every other boss beaten in single playthrough, zero respeccing, zero guides watched.[/spoiler] [h2][b]Story & Graphics and Environment[/b][/h2] Following the similar path as the previous [b]FromSoftware[/b] games, the [b]Elden Ring[/b] moves story forward via cutscenes and having conversations with NPC's. You won't get every necessary detail right away, but inspecting the environment, NPC's told stories and item texts, give you at least some knowledge of this vast, mystic and gruesome story and game lore. To get the whole picture, I recommend watching an video from YouTube after finishing the game. I will guarantee you'll be shocked to find some of the NPC lore and backgrounds later. The game doesn't include a "Quest-tracker" itself, but some guidance is provided by the map. This means you might accidentally skip some "cool side-quests". To those who really want to see every bit of story, I recommend following community tools like Wiki or YT videos. Once opening the first doors, you'll be welcomed to the 'the Lands Between'. The visuals and environment almost made me cry, for just being alive to experience this kind of magnificent graphical output. It's just so life-like and unreal at the same time. Being playing at the same time couple other open-world RPG games but their visual output isn’t even near what [b]Elden Ring[/b] is able to produce. Few YT channel recommendations (not all Lore related): [url=https://www.youtube.com/@VaatiVidya/videos]VaatiVidya[/url], [url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLVxgcx0CKkjo9lE40sUdRjhTHfF6XORub]Zullie the Witch[/url], [url=https://www.youtube.com/@ymfah/videos]ymfah[/url], [url=https://www.youtube.com/@Fextralife/playlists]Fextralife[/url]. [h2][b]Gameplay[/b][/h2] What can I say, the 'git gud' mentality will get you eventually. The game sets quite early that world isn't fair for you. You'll encounter many enemies and bosses with different movement, attack patterns alike, which some may be easy for your current build. Eventually you'll face the most absurd obstacle where it can get frustrated to continue. But be smart, learn from your mistakes and change/upgrade few things and brake through like a wrecking ball. Movement was the very key of my playthrough, and the Light/Medium armor sets felt at the end the best option. There is definitely better ways to play out than my way, but after unlocking certain "mixture", magic felt overpowered as I was able to Kamehame-haa the bosses straight to face and beat it under 10 seconds (this said thou I was also in some cases way above the enemies or the area level itself). Guarantee there is some even brain dead builds available on lower level to beat every boss of the game but that is the main aspect of the gameplay itself. You have the vast variety of options to move, attack, defend and ease the gameplay to the max if necessary. This is also the thing I'd like to see in other open-world RPG genre games in the future. [b]*Cough*, other AAA-game studios, please other take notes and put them into your games, but not behind a paywall.. Thank you.[/b] [h2][b]Soundtrack[/b][/h2] Once you start the game, your ears are going to bleed of liquefied diamonds. It is like a another dimension gods were living just to place every track preciously to time freeze bubble, so once you step inside of it. You're the one who lives the moment of an epic tale of the game. Soundtrack is an masterpiece of an composer work from [b]Tsukasa Saitoh, Shoi Miyazawa, Tai Tomisawa, Yuka Kitamura, and Yoshimi Kudo[/b] and the orchestra work from The Budapest Film Orchestra. Do check out the [url=https://bandainamco.lnk.to/Elden_Ring_ST]Official Soundtrack[/url] even if you haven't purchased the game yet. [h2][b]Conclusion[/b][/h2] [b]ELDEN RING is the best game ever made on year 2022 (and probably 2023).[/b] Buy it, play it, enjoy it, suffer from it and git gud you [b]Tarnished one[/b].

Questo gioco non è solo un Dark Souls in cui puoi saltare, è un open world originale e innovativo. Ogni dungeon, ogni singola zona di interesse da qualcosa di unico non randomico e realmente utile. Hai la sensazione che ogni singolo dungeon sia servito alla crescita del tuo personaggio e non perchè hai ottenuto 2 anime, 20 monete e 1 ciabatta in più di prima come in qualsiasi altro gioco, ma perchè hai ottenuto un oggetto che non avresti potuto trovare da nessun' altra parte e che potrebbe realmente servirti in futuro. Lo stile artistico è incredibile, ti fa dire "wow, che grafica pazzesca" anche se in realtà è una grafica di 5 anni fa, perciò non credete a chi dice che la grafica di Elden Ring è brutta perchè anche se dal lato tecnico non sorprende è comunque migliore di Dark Souls 3 ed è accompagnato da uno stile unico ed estremamente elaborato. Dal lato difficoltà non è una passeggiata ma poteva essere più difficile. Tolto il boss finale che credo di esserci arrivato sopralivellato avendo fatto letteralmente tutto prima di arrivarci, quindi credo sia normale mi fosse risultato troppo semplice, i boss dei dungeon secondari sono tipo 6 e vengono ripetuti più volte con qualche leggera modifica nell'arena e nelle mosse. Essendo di partenza non troppo difficili, capite che alla quinta volta che lo affronti è quasi un nemico normale, ANZI, certe volte lo diventa davvero. I boss di trama sono impegnativi, ma almeno io non credo di aver mai superato i 15 try con nessun boss. Gli unici boss che mi sono risultati davvero difficili, e quando dico difficili dico DIFFICILI, sono un boss opzionale e nascosto e un boss primario particolare dove dovresti evocare 5 - 6 persone ma l'ho voluto affrontare da solo, nessun altro. Tutti gli altri boss sono difficili solo se perdendovi nella mappa ci arrivate sotto livellati. Pecche del gioco? La magia. Oh, ogni arma che trovi 3 volte su 4 scala in fede. CHE PUALLE, ho capito l'albero ancestrale fatto di luce e sacro, ma cazzo se voglio fare una build no magia rispetto a chi ha fede e intelligenza posso usare 3 armi in croce, il coltello preso dalla cucina di Melina, una pantofola e i miei pugni. Ogni volta è un "Si, sapevo che c'era un dungeon qui" che finisce in un "si va beh ma che ca". Che poi sono pure fighe quelle armi, ma sono tutte in fede. MA a parte questo, le magie e le stregonerie sono rotte. Ho giocato insieme ad un mio amico con una build solo magia, io contro i boss con la mia build solo melee avevo una vera sfida, impegnativa e divertente, lui primo try, usa la magia da distanza, non ha bisogno di imparare il moveset dei boss perchè sta sempre lontano e fa comunque i miei stessi danni se non di più, easy gioco finito. In conclusione, gioco che merita, grande stile, impegnativo ma non esagerato come alcuni pensano, originale, estremamente rigiocabile, longevo e personalmente molto divertente. Alcuni mini boss sono troppo riciclati, le armi tendono troppo verso la fede e la magia è OP e rovina l'esperienza, ma non è niente rispetto ai moltissimi lati positivi che il gioco ha. Se vi piacciono gli open world rpg e non volete tutto servito su un piatto d'argento, è il gioco che fa per voi. Solo un consiglio, almeno per la prima run cercate di tendere al melee e non troppo alla magia, avrete un esperienza estremamente più divertente e soddisfacente

This being my first FromSoftware game, It was very difficults, but to my pleasant surprise, it actually ended up becoming one of my favorite games. even after many nights of feeling like a victim, wanting to break my setup and wanting to cry. The World My first playthrought I spent running straight into fights and regretting it soon later after i lost all my runes. I can't remember the last time I had this much fun just exploring and running around in a game's open world, and realizing the sheer scale of it all was exciting. Even if I had trouble with a boss or an area, I could just go somewhere else on the map until I felt ready to take it on. There's plenty of things to do before even beating the first story boss. Creature summons were also a huge help, and I was very happy with the options available. Trying out new weapons was fun, and even finding new ones for the lore bits was very compelling and made me want to collect them all. The Gameplay My first playthrough ended up being something like 120 hours long, though plenty of those hours were spent doing random things like climbing hard-to-reach places to enjoy the view or attempting to get most items. I also spent plenty of time stubbornly dying to enemies I wasn't quite yet ready to take on. The Multiplayer I asked for help from some friends at times, and there are a lot of funny moments to be had when playing with others. It's also not that difficult to find a random player to summon if you need help with a boss or dungeon. When you're in a boss arena, you can't be invaded, so if you're worried about that, you just have to limit summoning other players to when you're fighting bosses. Though honestly, the invading wasn't as scary as I'd expected, it was honestly kinda fun. I have some great memories from when me and my friend were invaded. Ending Thoughts I loved the npc's, although some of the quests felt like they ended too suddenly but others where extremly in detail and absolutly AMAZING. Seeing my character in cutscenes, however few, felt very satisfying. Especially as I can't help but dress up for that purpose alone lol. The only bad experience I really had with the game was towards the end. I absolutely hated a certain zones. The optional boss in the many areas are one of my favorite designs and one of my most memorable experiences in the game. Other than that, I had a few stutters here and there, but nothing too disrupting to my experience. Even if the game seems difficult, I think giving it a chance is really worth it. The game gives you a lot of options if you're struggling, and there are plenty of playstyles you can give a go. I went with Dual wielding Katanas (My favourite build, a Moonvaile and rivers of blood) Suffice to say, I'm super excited to see what the future dlc will bring and I highly recommend the game!

This is Dark Souls, but with an open world, and this is the biggest disappointment. The open world is not really interesting to explore and it serves only to move from one dungeon (or world boss) to the next one. And the dungeons and bosses are subpar to Dark Souls 1, I feel. Maybe that's because that game was groundbreaking in many aspects, and Elden Ring is just more of the same. In fact, it really feels like a remix of every other Soulsborne game, and the only new move is the ability to crouch ala Sekiro. There's nothing really innovative in terms of content: the weapons, the enemies, the location design - we've seen it in FromSoftware games before. Does this mean Elden Ring is a bad game? No, and I totally recommend it, but only because there's nothing else of the same quality on the horizon. But Elden Ring could have been so much more, so much better. Alas... Honestly, after finishing the game with 100% achievements and beating all key bosses (including Malenia), I can definitely say that the hardest enemies in the game (as in all other Soulsbornes) are camera, controls and performance. I thought 12900k and 3080Ti would be enough for 1440p gaming for a few more years, but no, FromSoftware managed to keep the videocard at 80-90% load at all times, with fps sometimes dropping to 40-50. And camera + controls is the same clunky stuff that I remember back from Dark Souls Prepare to Die Edition. Also, data streaming is really bad. Despite me having 32Gb RAM + 980 Evo Pro, sometimes the game totally froze when loading in a new part of the location. Well, in the end, it's part of the FromSoftware games DNA, I guess. If they were perfect, they would be too easy. In fact, Elden Ring is already much easier than Dark Souls 1/2/3 and Bloodborne, and even infamous Malenia is not that hard when you exploit her weaknesses (I killed her with a bloodloss build). For instance, it took me 80 hours to beat every key boss and do everything in Elden Ring, while the first Dark Souls took me 70 hours to beat, but I only killed one DLC boss out of three. And I played over 100 hours of Dark Souls 3 without getting all the achievements. So even though the game world looks massive, in terms of length Elden Ring is shorter than its predecessors due to lower difficulty. So, bottom line, a good Soulsborne game, much more user friendly than the previous ones, but not in any way groundbreaking.

My overall take: Wow. Where to even start. This is the first souls game I have ever played. I come from playing games like Destiny 2, Horizon Zero Dawn, Mass Effect, etc. Sometime the games being "hard". I did not know what hard was until I played this game. Nor have I ever had this much of challenge for a game. Other games are somewhat challenging, but this one tests your skills. Some of you will be slightly frustrated, some angry, and a select few give up the game when you keep trying to kill the sentinel at the starting area. But those who don't you will find yourself comparing other games to this game. Once you complete elden ring, every game you play after this will be a cake walk. This is a fantastic game. The world is so large with all sorts of enemies and items littered around the area. You actually have an incentive to explore in order to face the next boss. None of the quests are pointless skinned objectives. Every level up and item you get will bring you a step closer to becoming lord. Aspects: The parts that relieve you from the frustration is the messages on the ground. They can be helpful, but sometimes they can be funny and humorous. Read them when you have the chance. The number of main quests in this game aside from the linear story, are all meaningful and have purpose. The Items depending on your combat style will help you in your progress. Find Bell items to help get more items to level up your weapons. Explore the world. You spend plenty of time leveling up to get to the next boss. You might as well explore. The World: This game shows that art style is supreme when presenting a game. It may not be bringing your console or pc to its knees because of its graphics, but it beautiful in its own unique way. There will be times you just stop to admire how beautiful the game is. The world is so big. I didn't realize there was an underground area until mid way through my playthrough. There is so much in this world. You can spend hundreds of hours and you will never see all of it. Combat: Skill is everything. Be mindful and strategic. You can spam if you want but be strategic about it. Find the way you like to fight at the beginning of the game and not further in. I learned using a regular axe of the most the way until midway then I switched weapon type and took some time to learn. Long story short find the way you like to fight and stick with it, while improving your skills. End Review: I have never played a game that required this much skill. I was frustrated many times, but when you beat a boss it is so rewarding and feels great. I hope you all enjoy the journey to become the Elden Lord.

I got this game when it first came out. I reached Stormveil (the first 'stronghold' area) while streaming to my friends (all of whom were super deep into the game already), and after getting lots of super in-depth tips from them, I rage quit after some bullshit (a friendly NPC steals your runes every time you die in his area, and I ended up going broke and losing all the souls I got from the 2 big previous bosses). After that, I uninstalled Elden Ring and didn't play it for a whole year. I thought about leaving a negative review for a while, because the experience I had first playing this game was dog shit, with too many secrets and too much emphasis on getting your time wasted fucking around and finding out. A year later, I've dusted Elden Ring off to give it another try, except this time I played it my way. I didn't let anyone tell me what the "objectively best starting class" is, or take advice on what build to make, or which direction to go after I spawned. I just ran towards whichever horizon I wanted, killed what I met, ran away if I couldn't, looked up whatever guides I needed to to avoid wasting time with groundhog day-esque death-heavy puzzle segments. It was an entirely different experience, and said experience is the only way I can really recommend you play this game. If you're going to play Elden Ring, do it the way you want to, and try to limit the number of outside voices telling you how you should be playing. There's a huge temptation to, just like in Tarkov, let Reddit-dwellers (or your friends in VC) do the thinking for you and tell you what you should be using for the most DPS or whatever - don't do this. Don't let elitist slimes tell you that you have to fight every boss head on either, or that you can't use summons, or that magic is 'gay', or that you shouldn't play any starting class besides the Samurai. Use however many quest guides or maps you feel you need, and just experience the fucking game with the features it has, in any combination that you want. If you're someone that gets frustrated when a seemingly meaningless decision causes something disastrous to happen, make sure to look up each NPC you meet to see if they're someone who's going to help or hinder you. Oh and the story sucks, so stick to being impressed by visuals and cool weapons rather than by trying to make sense of all the dumb names and plotlines.

This review is written from a (perspective) run I tried to do with a standard classic greatsword playthru with no summons, incarnation,passive buildups which open up my eyes on ER flaws a lot more: The Main Bosses aka the Legendary Bosses that you are required to beat are honestly not that fun or satisfying. It seem like they all share the same type of behaviour: -spam every attack possible with little to no cooldown in-between each attack and ability. -leave a 0.5 second window for the player to both react on and deal damage in -Evade if the player is close to them for more then 2 seconds. -have a back/tail attack if you manage to out-maneuver them and strike from behind. -Still being able to instantly kill you even with 60+ Vigor. And even when you manage to outplay them they will find a way to punish you. Out of all main bosses that I played against the only ones that was fun more me was Godfrey and Rykard. The mid to late game bosses are some of the most dull and annoying encounters as well: Radahn: Honestly not the worst but just feel like a chore if anything. Draconic Tree sentinel: I mean its already a tree sentinel reskin with just some added abilites that they spam even more with. Morgott: Spam and very small attack windows if you try to avoid damage. Fire giant: ridiculous large arena and tanky HP. You are not even fighting a boss, just its feet. God skin duo: Reskin fight of the Godskins noble but you have to fight 2 instead of just 1 and you need to kill both of them twice. Makelith. Spam. There is to much waiting and too little combat cause of all the spam attacks and Evades. This also leaves a lot of weapon types unviable for PVE cause of how slow you attack with them. By the time you started your swing animation with something like a colossal sword the boss could already gotten 5 hits on you. I am not saying its impossible to beat them with standard "balanced true-soul experience gameplay" builds But its not fun Fromsoftware balanced the game way to much around co-op and arcane/int/ability builds it indirectly nerfed standard sword and no-abilites meele gameplay which is a bummer. On my first playthrough all I used was a katana with bleed buildup and scarlet rot dragon ability and it was pretty much ggs. +Game is still really fun +there is so much to do +Good replayability +Fun and intresting side quests as well side quest bosses +tons of different builds and playstyles you can do and test out (even if some of them are straight up busted or really underwhelming without specific items) In the end of the day ER is primarily a RPG game so it make sense to a degree the way its balanced and designed If you however want something that offer a more linear and rewarding basic melee gameplay you should probably look into DS3 or Sekiro.

Gone is the challenging yet fair game-play of their previous games. My second gripe is the open-world aspect. It's so boring! There's not enough in it to actually explore, so you're essentially just running from one major area to another, with a few bits and pieces in between. The atmosphere and the look of the world is great though. Elden Ring would've benefited so much more from proper interconnected world design. Nearly everything else is also just copy pasted from previous games, the combat, the animations etc. I'd say if this is your first From Software game, you may enjoy it, but, I would suggest you play Dark Souls 1 and/or Bloodborne instead.

The first 40 hours of the game are honestly the best experience I've had in a while and I wouldn't trade it for anything else. There is a reason why I said the first 40 hours though, after leaving the capital city, Leyndell, the quality takes a dip. And a DIP at that. Most bosses I saw in very special places and got to fight at the end of long questlines are just in mines and out in the open just sitting there for no reason. In the early game whenever I got to see a big enemy I always wanted to fight and best them but in the snow covered mountaintops all I've ever done is just wave past with Torrent. I think the issues in the game can be fixed, but the community's point of view towards issues are also something to be wary of. The "hardest" fight, Malenia, is barely hard if you're using every tool the game gives you to beat her. The reason a lot of the bosses in the game feel like they were made for Sekiro and not Elden Ring and there being no way (literally no way, like there isn't a single way you don't take damage in some bosses' attacks) is because you aren't using Spirit Ashes to pull aggro from the boss, which seems like that's what they were balanced towards. However, I will agree that spirit ashes feel like you're "cheating" towards the latter stages of the game (especially mimic) and balancing them will no doubt prove extremely difficult for FromSoftware. NOTE: I played this game at launch. It's okay. This review will compare Elden Ring to Dark Souls III a lot for obvious reasons. The open world formula hurts this game a lot. A sense of bewilderment is common when you move around with barely any direction at all. You get indications to sites of grace, but that's it. When i tried going someplace interesting on my own i got stomped instantly. If i didn't explore the crevices of the vast empty land, i was under leveled. If i explored everything then i saw the same ruins asset and enemies scattered everywhere. It felt like a grind and exploration for the sake of exploration. When i moved on to the "correct" path, and there certainly is one, although the game nor the players tell you that, it all felt very good. The pacing was amazing. This harkens back to my previous statement; when the developer guides you in and puts you through the curated experience (i.e you play it like Dark Souls 3), it's really, really good. When you actually do open world content, it actually kind of sucks. A huge flaw in design for me is the way they introduce you this danger. Spoilers: There is a point in the game where you get transported from the starting zone, to a much higher level Zone, Caelid. It's very obvious you are supposed to, and should, run. So i did. I got to a site of grace and went back home. This is introduced if you enter an obscure cave with a chest at the end. The run where i didn't do this, and entered as i normally would with Torrent, i got stomped by the enemies and lost my runes. Therefore, it's apparent to me that the game is made to be explored and scoured for treasure. However, this content is repetitive. The same reused caves and bosses are littered across the map and give you cool stuff. The enemies here are annoying and the same in all of them, with varying layouts. Completing these is mostly a chore you do to unlock things. Not once did i do a dungeon and find it a refreshing or interesting experience. Oh, and if you skip all these you will likely be under leveled and miss out on all the cool stuff. Following the curated experience is good. I wish they had taken more steps to gently guide you in game instead so they could lean into what they do best, the "dancing" with the bosses. Dark Souls 3 had exquisite combat flow and each boss had a built-in rythm to learn, with few exceptions (looking at you, Oceiros). The satisfaction from completely dismantling a boss by learning their every move was amazing. It truly felt like you rose from the ashes and became stronger by learning every time. The bosses in Elden Ring attack you so mercilessly that you offload some hits to your summons instead or just abuse magic so you avoid the combat. The openings you gain are therefore the boss attacking your meatshield instead of your own skill dodging their attacks and abusing these openings, especially if you use heavy weapons. I repeat, the intended way to play the game is by not interacting with the boss. To see the anthisesis of this, and my ideal version of the game, look at the Iudex Gundyr or Dragonslayer Armor fight from Dark Souls 3. To summarize, I feel the design around summons and the bosses are poorly done. Removing summons in boss fights, if not altogether, would drastically improve the game. There is no option to not use summons unless you want to use exploits, metagame or otherwise play OP builds, and not what you find fun. The weapons and ashes of war are good. The combat is better with more variation and more moves to learn. The progression is there. TL;DR The game is okay, but ultimately dissapointing coming from Dark Souls 3. Two steps forward in some directions, two steps back in others.
