Fifteen hours into Elden Ring, I defeated Godrick, the first of five Elden Lords. In the time between emerging into the Lands Between and striking him down, I'd discovered decrepit ruins, ventured into twisting caves, stumbled upon enemy encampments, and battled tooth and nail against challenging bosses. From Software's games have always made you feel small in many ways: They tell you that you're worthless--a plague-ridden rat or accursed Undead, unfit even to be cinders. They ask you to navigate unflinching brutal worlds and pit you against enemies that systematically dismantle your ego. Elden Ring maintains the nail-biting combat and air of mystery that has distinguished From Software's Soulsborne games, but it's elevated to new heights by the studio's interpretation of what an open-world game can be. Having brought down Godrick, the breadth of the world--and the way in which From Software has applied its signature style to an open world--was on full display, reinforcing how insignificant I really was and driving home the magnitude of the task that still awaited me. Standing on the edge of a cliffside in Liurnia of the Lakes, the area beyond Godrick's arena, I took in the world laid out in front of me: the enormous Erdtree casting brilliant golden beams of light onto the land that exists in its shadow; the sharp peaks of a distant mountain that look like claws tearing at the sky; a castle standing proudly amidst ruins; a forest blanketed in an ominous fog. It was all overwhelming, and none of the hardships I'd experienced in Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, or Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice have come close to making me feel as small. At the same time, I was overcome with excitement for what the Lands Between had in store for me and all the seemingly insurmountable battles awaiting--and it did not disappoint. Elden Ring is From Software's crowning achievement in world design--epic in scale and scope. But what makes it special isn't just how visually stunning it all is, or that its open-world is vast, rich in detail, and teeming with possibilities. Instead, it's how the studio has applied its own esoteric design principles to deliver an experience that feels fresh, elegant, and uniquely From Software. The game's core pillars are built on the same strong action and role-playing foundations as previous titles while offering more freedom to explore than ever before. Elden Ring is an open-world game entirely in a category of its own. That delicate orchestration of highs and lows and the build-up and release of tension that From Software has mastered, coupled with the thrill of freeform exploration and discovery, is an intoxicating cocktail of game design. In guiding the player, Elden Ring employs the lightest of touches. The Lands Between is truly open and offers the player complete agency in exploration, whether on foot or horseback. The world is ruled by five Elden Lords, each in possession of a shard of the titular Elden Ring. As a lowly Tarnished, you aim to defeat these corrupt lords, take their shards, stand before the Erdtree, and become an Elden Lord in your own right. With the premise established through a quick cutscene, you are let loose and left to forge a path through the world as you see fit. A key part of From Software's design ethos is to strip down to the essentials, and in Elden Ring that process strengthens exploration and discovery, the heart and soul of the experience. The studio's games typically give the player very little while asking a lot, and Elden Ring is the most obtuse and demanding of its games so far. This is largely because everything you've come to expect from modern open-world games is absent; for instance, there's no map until you find an item that reveals the topography of a region. Even then, the points of interest in that region aren't marked until you've been there and seen them. There is no minimap, just a compass to show the cardinal directions and any waypoints you've placed. Characters, meanwhile, aren't desperate for your attention; as with previous games, the quests they task you with aren't noted down or tracked in any kind of log--it's up to you to do your due diligence. Areas you go to won't be gated depending on your level, and there's no clear indication on when you should go to key locations. The best you get is at the Sites of Grace, which function as rest points in the same way Bonfires, Lanterns, or Idols did in other titles. At each of these sites is a dim trail of golden light pointing in the general direction of… something. Perhaps it's the next milestone in your quest or maybe it's just another area that has a dungeon--the only way to find out is to make the journey. The challenge for From Software lies in the friction between the studio's design hallmarks and the expected conventions of a genre filled with games that try to be all things to everyone. And although the execution is an unmitigated success, one thing's for sure: Elden Ring is not a smooth-edged, one-size-fits-all kind of experience that will accommodate everyone. Instead, it's unrelentingly opaque, relishes in the savagery of confronting players with unfavorable odds, and delights in watching the ensuing struggle. Elden Ring's gameplay will feel familiar to those with experience of previous From Software games. The tried-and-true formula of measured third-person combat against enemies that are swift to punish foolhardiness is both as thrilling and nerve-racking as ever. Whether you wield a sword and shield, swing something that's closer to a heap of raw iron, or stand back as a mage and launch spells to topple your foes, Elden Ring tests patience and skill with tricky enemy mobs and ferocious bosses.

World is very open; you get a convenient mount early to make the huge map feel appropriate. Most boss fights seem to allow you to run away if it's a lot more than you expected, which also prevents the loss/death/abandonment/rage quit spirals. There are plenty of areas to grind if you'd rather not get as good at the mechanics. I wish the player character sketched in the map as you traversed it. I wish it didn't have an always online requiement. I would rather have a more casual entirely single player experience. The game is not perfect. But it is the most aesthetic game I've seen in a very long time; often it looks like the screenshot belongs in a museum. And of all the Dark Souls games, this does seem to be in the more forgiving half, which is great because I don't enjoy the more hardcore half. Unlike Dark Souls the game has legit magic. It is still a hack and slash first, but the magic is well developed and can be used a lot, especiallly if you spec into it. With both healing and destruction spells, it covers the basis and there might be more interesting spells I haven't gotten to or been killed by a random invader with. As an RPG and action adventure player, this game is great. Like I said, it's a bit hard and there's nothing to do but grind. I won't fault it since it's a design decision and I don't mind grinding. If you aren't skilled, don't want to die often, and don't like grinding, you should avoid this like the plague. If you are fine with just one of them, I'd buy it at least on-sale. Of course, if you like Dark Souls, I'm sure you already bought this so just play it already.

I quantify my appreciation for this game in comparing it to Witcher 3, a game I played up to the hardest setting 'Death March' and logged over 1000 hrs. In the first 30 minutes of Witcher 3 I found the game to be fun, interesting, and wishing to play more. In the first 30 minutes of Elden Ring I found myself asking how is it I avoid dying in combat to exacting parry timers, advanced enemy AI, and vague scaling in enemy strength. At this point I've cleared the Tree Sentinel and three minor bosses in caves, in lieu of satisfaction of achievement it's just the relief of one less thing trying to chase me down and kill me. The encumbering system of relying on potions to recover and hoping to find the next respawn point mirrors the relief as treading water is a reality because everything respawns if you rest to refill the potions which can place a drag on progress. I am skeptical that I will finish the game with the trend it carries on with. I would say this game appeals to people who enjoy balancing on the edge of a knife, because it doesn't seem meant for the average gamer. I had wondered why there were rage videos on Youtube for the game, while I can't say a game can incline me to such a response now I can feel sympathy for their irritation.

Once in a great while, a game comes along that seamlessly combines impeccable gameplay, a wondrous world, incredible tone-setting music, and unparalleled art direction. That game is From Software’s Elden Ring, an action RPG that channels the best aspects of the genre. This absurdly ambitious open world captivated my curiosity, enticed me with puzzles, secrets, and mysteries, and served up unbelievably satisfying moments as I experienced one of the most extraordinary adventures of all time. From my initial foray into the world to the final moments, every step of the journey is a note in a personalized epic that kept me coming back for more. The Lands Between is a world full of discovery, and while a clear path forward exists for those seeking guidance, roaming the lands unfettered without a particular goal in mind often yields surprises. I often had a spot to explore marked on my map and got off-track along the way, sometimes leading to entirely new areas and feature-dense zones. The grandiose world is chock full of characters, quests, and various dungeon crawls ranging from tiny catacombs to massive multilayered tombs. While the journey starts with little caves, mines, and other dungeon delves, these experiences become more complex. Two-room affairs eventually become intricate teleport puzzles or scenarios where you discover unusual ways to interact with the environment, like learning to use traps for traversal or sniffing out secret walls. Your character is incredibly customizable, which I found highly rewarding. You can attach various skills and scaling mechanics across the board, allowing you to truly create your own vision of a traveling hero. Respecialization and alterations allow you to finely tweak your creation without worrying too much about experimentation along the way as you arm yourself with everything from explosive pots to potent perfumes to complement your ever-growing arsenal. The open world is majestic, dripping with flavor and atmosphere, and full of fabulous finds. However, the legacy dungeons are the stuff of legend, often connecting to the outside from multiple points. These curated sprawls are a dream to dissect, and Elden Ring often offers different ways to maneuver through these areas. The big bosses, generally found at the end of legacy dungeons, feel like wonderful wars against demigods. These brilliant set piece battles are thrilling exclamation points to an outrageous odyssey, absolute spectacles, and masterful combinations of tension and triumph. Elden Ring has the distinction of having the best and most challenging boss battle in any From Software game to date. Hidden away and optional, this encounter had me waking up in the middle of the night to come back and crash against its beautiful and terrifying destruction over and over again. After finally besting this opponent, I let loose a triumphant victory roar there while sitting in the dark and wearing my pajamas, wanting nothing more than to experience the encounter again. This example speaks to how unbelievably compelling and immersive Elden Ring is; I regularly put it down with the intent of doing something else and found myself back within minutes. There is always one more gnawing mystery to unravel, one more boss to beat, and one more hidden route to find. Elden Ring challenged me, captivated me, and enchanted me, an unyielding deluge of discovery and artistic vision unbound. Elden Ring represents a truly amazing combination of various game elements that all come together to create something fascinating, special, and unforgettable. Elden Ring isn’t just the best game this year; it’s one of the best games ever made.

Do I recommend this game? Yes and no. Why the "no"? It's not a game meant for everyone, and I mean that. It is a challenging game, and can be extremely frustrating at times. However, if you like to be challenged, if you enjoy the feeling after overcoming a difficult fight, then this is for you. The lore is not an in your face type of story. You've got to do some digging. I suggest reading item descriptions, it goes a LONG way in clarifying the story, as well as exploring and going off the beaten path. As someone who played DS3 (a LOT), I absolutely love this game and the story. It's dark, gritty, and most of all sad; but it is compelling. It draws you in and throws you for a loop. Gameplay wise, it runs smoothly, and I have no issues. Controls are nearly the same as Dark Souls 3 (with the addition of jumping). I don't suffer from my game CTD'ing (crash to desktop) or anything. In terms of style of play, there are a lot of different builds. More than just the spell slinger or sword and board styles. It's fun, interesting and I enjoy the freedom of it. Some builds (scarlet rot/bleed) are OP, that mainly applies to multiplayer/pvp and less so for solo play. Overall, is it worth the pricetag on it? Absolutely, worth the buy.

Elden Ring operates on one simple idea: You, a weak and frail nobody, have to rise to the occasion and slay hideous monsters, gigantic dragons, legendary kings, ancient gods, and even ferocious madness-inflicting rats in order to accomplish your goals. This is quickly and efficiently established as you unsuspectingly start the game and immediately get splattered across the walls by a sword wielding, acid spewing spider made out of corpses. You have now discovered that you're in a brutal and apathetic environment that will try to kill you regardless of your complaints. When you mull over that synopsis, what comes to mind? It sounds unfair, doesn't it? Every aspect of the game is specifically designed to be an obstacle against your progress that you have to overcome, to the point of feeling unfair at many points. And at some points, it is actually unfair. But the task this game demands of you is to put your boots on and push through every obstacle until you finally overcome them, leading to a feeling of accomplishment that wouldn't be there if you just beat the boss in one try. The basic framework of the gameplay is deceivingly simple, you either attack your enemy, or dodge their attack, but in actuality you will have to consider many aspects like positioning, health and stamina, length and moveset of your weapon, and learn to avoid fatal beginner mistakes like overcommitting on your attacks or panic dodges that get easily punished by your enemies. The map of the game is truly massive, it is the one of the few, perhaps even the only detailed video game environments that provides a true sense of scale. You see that giant tree? That's not the skybox, that's where you're going. Over the course of the game you will traverse massive lakes, great forests, gargantuan castles, deep and ancient underground cities, and mountainous mountains. Elden Ring succeeds where most open world games fail by being a vertical game, you will be able to visit the highest heights and the lowest depths. Unfortunately, due to the scale of the world, from a loot perspective exploration is not rewarded nearly as well as previous Fromsoft games. In Dark Souls when you searched through the cracks and crevices of a location off the beaten path you would end up finding a cool sword or armor set, but in Elden Ring it's more likely to be a mushroom for crafting. While this is a valid complaint it's also simply not feasible for the developers to have gone and placed unique items at every little hidden cliffside or dead end. But if you personally enjoy exploration for its own sake and seeing the incredible sights of the game then you won't have any problems. The most controversial aspect of the game is the multiplayer. The way it works is that you can summon friends into your game to explore together and help you fight enemies. The co-op can be a bit inconvenient because the game doesn't let you go between separate map areas in multiplayer, and it doesn't let you use your horse in multiplayer either. The part where people are divided though is the invasion system. When you are playing with friends, another player can invade your world and attempt to kill you in order to halt your progress. Many people buy Fromsoft games thinking that they are exclusively a PvE experience and then encounter invaders and it leaves a sour taste in their mouth. The problems people have with invaders range from simply not enjoying having their progress halted by another person, to many invaders using broken meta weapons that are very difficult to counter. To me, this issue with invaders is closely related to the core philosophy of the game. Just like a difficult boss, invaders are yet another obstacle to your quest that the game mercilessly throws at you. Invaders also have their own obstacles, the game throws teams of 2-3 people at them and they have to be good enough to handle the pressure and use their environment as an advantage in their war of attrition. From the invader's perspective, the host and their summons are the boss that must be overcome. Though I prefer the gameplay, in my opinion as a whole the PvP in this game is a step down from Dark Souls 3. The previous games had a system called covenants, which were essentially factions that a player could choose that had unique matchmaking and item rewards for co-op and PvP. This system is only just barely present in Elden Ring, and it's watered down. Even in the previous games the rewards for multiplayer weren't that good but now you essentially get nothing except for a good time. The only thing resembling a covenant left in the game are the white and blue cipher rings that respectively allow you to call for help from another player whenever you get invaded or respond to that call for help. TLDR: This game sucks you in and transports you into a brutal yet beautiful world of fantasy, borrowing heavily from Lord of The Rings and Berserk. 10/10 would solo her again.

I write this review as I have 100% completed Elden Ring. And yet, despite this, I still find new things every time I play the game. Elden Ring is an experience to say the least, and I won't be dramatic and say it is life changing but it feels like this is THE video game to play if you're ever going to play a game. It's immersive and full of story, every little thing is made with such refined detail that you can easily miss the little things. Everything feels so interconnected and it is so easy to get lost and find yourself on an adventure. It's been a long time since I've felt like a game really wanted me to just... go explore and have fun with the world. It feels punishing but no punishment in this game goes unrewarded. Here's my breakdown of the game, I'll try not to spoil but I'll post spoiler warnings just in case. *Story*: As any Fromsoft game is, the world is vague and extremely open ended. Which can be a huge mess if done wrong but this is done entirely right. Story is not handed to you on a silver platter, however if you do wish to go find it through character storylines, you're given plenty of exposition and development. Characters are made to make you care about them or hate them. A lot. Where Elden Ring shines is the characters that they weave into the story and how important bosses feel to kill due to story context. The context you are given bit by bit really sell your journey. *The Endings*: (I have not done Golden Mask or Dungeater's ending as they do not really interest me too much. Do note there are spoilers up ahead so skip this section if you don't want that) -Ranni's Ending was actually one of the most satisfying endings to a Souls game I've seen in a long time. She was a compelling character and her roster of companions feel fun and diverse in their own ways. They take you on this meaningful journey with twists and questionable moral choices. And to wrap it all up nicely after taking you underground to Nokron, Fromsoft has you revisiting areas previously to ground you in Ranni's backstory via Liurnia. I 100% recommend getting this ending and I'll be posting a guide soon! -Frenzy Flame Ending was... something? It wasn't exactly remarkable but I did really enjoy the voice acting! I can't say the way to get it was entertaining though, go through some sewers, comet azur Mohg, and take 5 minutes to jump on some graves and now you have an ending only 15% of people this game have. It didn't feel satisfying but it was visually neat and the eyes look really radical. -Elden Lord. Nuff said, you become elden lord. A decent neutral ending! -Fia's. This one was actually really mysterious and fun. Full of deceit and conflict. You don't get an achievement with this alas but it's worth doing. Fun bosses, neat story, Fia being based. *Gameplay* It takes some getting used to. I grew up on the souls games and I am used to fast paced movements. But I really had to be patient with this one! Lots of delay which forces you to pay attention to the details of certain bosses. Also adding jumping in with some of the mechanics was really neat! Albeit a bit annoying from time to time (Cough, Godfrey, Cough). The dungeons and caves are plenty of fun and remind me of old legend of zelda mechanics. The bosses are fun and engaging, always on your toes. Although Rennala was a slight bore phase 1. You can take your time or zoom through the Main Story. Going back to back in the story takes around 2-4 hours. But there's so much to do in the game that it might take you 100+ hours to even complete it. So, yeah. Play it.

I'm a bit of a cheapskate, not to mention my taste in video games tends to steer me away from the $60 triple-a titles. I'm also not usually the biggest fan of open world games either. They often tend to have way too much wide open space or have a bunch of boring npcs with even more boring quests. However I enjoyed Dark Souls III enough to take a gamble on this one. I'm very glad I did. This game respects my monkey brain of "I wanna run around and kill stuff" more than any other open world or RPG ever has. While the large set pieces are the stars of the show, likely due to their more linear dark souls-y design, the open areas still have plenty of activities, and the exploration feels very organic, so it never feels like going from point A to point B, but rather "that building in the distance sure looks interesting, I'll head in that general direction while checking out stuff on the side." I feel like my $60 has already been worth it, and I've barely made a dent in this game. Edit: 60 hours in and I do have a few criticisms. 1. The pvp kinda sucks. There's no more random invasions except during co-op, which encourages invaders to be more toxic, since there's a higher likelihood that they'll get 3v1'd. 2. The game feels way easier than previous souls games. I had a little trouble in the early game but once I got my build settled I've pretty much been steamrolling everything. 3. There's a lot of copy/paste. I don't mind the repeated enemies and minibosses so much, since there's plenty of other solid games that do similar things. My big gripe is with some of the later game mini-dungeon layouts, which overuse the trope of "ooo, this layout of rooms is exactly the same as the ones you just went through, oooo, what a labyrinth, you feel lost yet?" like bruh I though we had stopped doing that shit back in the NES era because we all agreed it wasn't fun. It's fine for like, one or two dungeons as a gimmick, but it got old fairly quick. All that being said, the game is still an incredibly good time, and I'll certainly be seeing it through till the end.

This game is definitely a worthwhile playthrough for anyone who may take the slightest interest in this genre. Though, I must say this game's end game does not have the most polish when compared to the beginning of the game. Bosses are overly punishing and overly active. The philosophy of bosses seems to have been very muddied. Bosses with large health pulls will have attacks capable of nearly one-shotting any build that does not dump vigor. Most early-game bosses are challenging, but well made enough to be beaten at any point in the game depending on skill level. The later bosses are very different on the other hand. The over-aggressive nature of bosses and their habit to end combos just to immediately begin a new one before you can properly achieve a hit is an incredibly frustrating one. Leaving you to always be overly cautious in order to even get an attack in. Forcing the players to constantly be on the defensive and break the flow of combat creates a less interesting environment and gameplay loop. It seems like the developers decided to focus on making the bosses more "challenging" rather than fun. Bosses being challenging is a perfectly fine mechanic and is fundamental to the franchise, but Elden Ring seems to tip the scales, several times, into the frustrating territory. Having to wait an entire Youtube Ad's length of time for a proper opening in a boss only to do minimal damage is just not a fun way to play the game. Spending several minutes whittling a massive health bar, only to be instantly killed by singular mistake is not a fun way to play a game. Bosses with small health pools that are incredibly punishing are completely fine and enjoyable challenges. Bosses with massive health pools that spend most of their time whittling you down for your mistakes over time are also completely fine and enjoyable. It's when the two are mixed, is when you create an overall frustrating experience. Do not get me wrong. I love this game and enjoyed the many hours I put into it, but the game's late game bosses make it a difficult choice to want to replay it. 7/10 game trapped in a 10/10 frame. I would love to see this game get a sequel that irons out the issues.

I'm going to lead with the fact that this is my favorite souls game by significant margin. I have played, enjoyed, and look back fondly on the entire franchise, but something about the first play-through of this game makes the rest look paltry in comparison. Elden Ring takes a franchise renown for its depressing mood, Incredible level design and fair but brutal combat and turns it on its head in one of my favorite reimaginings since Jak 2 on the PS2. Tight corridors and claustrophobia have been replaced with a vast open world, dotted with some of the most intricate and brutal zones the franchise has ever presented in the form of Legacy Dungeons. Out in the open world itself, you'll find yourself exploring a series of wondrous and alien environments filled with the remnants of once great civilizations, as well as a variety of World Bosses, Dungeons, Puzzles, Gear, and every assortment of goody the game has to offer. There is a degree of repetition to this game, in that some tile sets and bosses can be a little... overused at times. However, I cannot stress the shear scope of this game. I highly recommend playing without spoiling the map, as its truly a treat to watch the world unfold. On the same note, visually speaking, this is not the most hyper realistic game you'll ever see. However, it compensates in that it is still ABSOLUTELY GORGEOUS. From Soft is known for its vistas and "wow" moments, and this game takes that to a new degree by constantly making you look around in sheer wonder. From the color scheme to the world design, From Soft manages to take all the ideas that made them famous and redefine them by a golden standard. Difficulty remains a controversial issue, but I think this is just the right difficulty. If you steamroll ahead, following the Graces and progressing the story alone, you will run into nigh insurmountable odds that will bring on a sweat for even the saltiest souls vet. However, unlike before, you have a massive area full of side content to enrich, empower, and add variety to your combat style, and it will have you tossing bombs, slinging knives, and upgrading that new sword you found in a cave to overcome these massive spikes with a natural ease that reeks of a masterpiece. Truly, this stands next to Bloodborne and DS3 as masterclasses in the genre, but unlike those, it marks a moment of progression for the series, breaking free from several of its bonds and paving the way for even greater things to follow. Keep an eye out for the next From "Souls" game, its going to make this one look terrible. 10/10, so good I even got 100%.

TLDR: Everybody knows this game is good, you don't need me to tell you. If you're afraid it's too difficult for you, there are strategies to make the game easier. If you have the money and the time to spend on this game, it will be worth them both, trust me. My experience: That said, as a souls fan, I didn't feel like this game really attended my expectations (which to be fair where problaby very high). It's weird to describe: part of me loved this game, but another part of me was also expecting something else, or for things to be different about it, I don't know. Probably the biggest part of the insatisfaction I have with this game is the "level-scaling system" (for lack of a better term. It's actually the interaction of the XP system with the open word system): because it's such an open game, you end up missing entire areas when you're at their intended level, and when you actually find them, those areas are way too easy for you. This happened so much so that I had this doubt of having my level way too low/high throughout basically the whole game. Not only is this the first time I feel that in a souls game, it is also really annoying, because you always have that feeling in your head: "Damn, this boss was so hard, was my level way too low for him?" or, even worse: "This boss was so easy! I guess my level is way too high for this section of the game" (the latter happened to me more often, which is a shame). This happens mostly with the optional bosses, but having this constant thought in my head really detracted from my experience, I believe. Overall I think the openness of the map as opposed to previous titles was a double-edge sword: It provided incredible moments of wanderlust and exploration, but also made me not enjoy the main parts of the game as much.

im saying this is gonna be a pretty long review. next thing i want to talk about are the bosses, this game would absolutely not be complete with the countless challenging (yet annoying) bosses, but i really appreciate the fact that the developers didn't make it so if you encounter a boss that you can't beat you have to spend hours, days, or even weeks trying to so you can progress in the story, first encountered maliketh there was a draconic tree sentinel in front of his boss room, i spent nearly an hour trying to defeat them, only to enter the boss room and kill maliketh in a few minutes, this is the kind of shit i talk about when i say "balancing issues". pacing and guidance: now when i first started the game i remember accidentally roaming to the mid-game part of the map, to say the and following the grace paths are the only decent guides you get at the start of the game and even if you figure that out those options barely work. for the rest of the game you're fated to just listen to the boring, bland dialogue of what to do or where to go not even knowing if you're supposed to listen to that advice due to you not understanding where to travel to next because of how Note: This is not strictly a negative review, but the game’s overall design makes it hard for me to openly recommend it. Elden Ring is an open world combat RPG, where battling with enemies is the center of everything. There is a huge world to explore where you find various items, that help your character you make in the beginning to become stronger statistically, but everything you find centers on your combat capability of course, since this is not an adventure game. Albeit this approach, the game offers some impressive vistas throughout the world you explore, somewhat curious NPCs that talk to you and most importantly challenges in the form of varying enemies and boss battles. There are many places you can visit, also underground, which all help you, at the end of the day, to become stronger by giving you more runes, that are basically a currency you buy levels with at checkpoints. If one is familiar with the developer’s, From Software, former titles, the risk reward mechanic is the same in here and the actual fighting mechanics are also the same as in Dark Souls games; you lose your runes when you die, but can retrieve them from your death spot, but lose them completely if you die again before that, and the fighting is basically careful observing of enemies while dodging (by rolling endlessly) and blocking. The game is fun at the beginning, offering decent challenge, and at any point if you find the game too tough, which is likely, you can gain more levels by collecting runes for slaying enemies or simply exploring easier approachable areas. Since the game is very long in length due to the sheer size of the world, most players might wish to follow the main path straight to the end without much additional exploration, but alas, the game’s difficulty, even despite the help of a selectable phantom fighter (spirit ashes) who you can call in for help in tough spots, forces exploration to gain runes for the vast majority of players to overcome later tough enemies. This might not sound like an issue, since this applies to some other open world titles too, but the time it takes to explore to be strong enough is in tens of hours – I’m not exaggerating. While the beginning is fun and quite exciting, the more you play the more repetition kicks in, even if the areas around the map are visually different, but enemies repeat and so do bosses; they use the same models. Even the overall quality of level design is better at the beginning, the Stormveil Castle being at least to me the most exciting place to see and explore, after that perhaps a few notable places existing in the game. This castle is at the very beginning and after that the quality slowly drops the further you get, endgame being very tough and a slog to get through, mostly due to some nasty bosses. The bosses are a big part of the studio’s focus and they are admittedly often fun to fight, but in this game most bosses are annoyingly designed, scaling in damage too much from the very beginning till the end. This vast damage they tend to inflict in a single strike makes the game more a hectic rhythm based act to avoid the worst hits, while waiting patiently for an opening to strike pretty much freely when the enemy takes it’s pause. I find this limiting character building wise, since I’m sure the game is extremely hard without putting many skill points on vitality (max health) to sustain more damage. The bosses also have cheap moves and combos, which often rightfully makes you feel like you die an unexpected and unfair death, but this is thankfully mitigated by the phantom helper that can take hits from enemies instead of you and even slightly damage them, so you can heal up on the side, perhaps cast a spell or incantation and prepare to strike again. So even if boss design is most often not as great as in previous games from the studio, especially compared to Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, occasionally being even bad, the phantom helper is there for you making some bosses actually pretty trivial, which is not a bad thing if you don’t wish to be stuck on them in this - in my honest opinion - too long game. I personally have explored almost everything in the world and I’m likely ”over leveled”, which would mean that in the main progression path I’m fighting enemies on a higher level than players usually are, but still, after playing so long, easily over 100 hours in fact, I’m still currently momentarily stuck at one mandatory very late game boss that, once again, has upped damage so that it can kill you in a short sweep of attacks. This fact is saddening to me, since the game has pretty fun exploration, the best yet character building in the studio’s history, amusing places to discover, and of course the action is intuitive and most often entertaining, but yet the game is enough of a slog to get through at many points and too repetitive. If you decide or rather need to explore much because of the difficulty that can spike, the game starts undoubtedly to feel overall as following: cheap. It is a cheap game in the end with talent and quality at many places, but filler content and bad design all over the place. This game should have been shorter in my opinion, or at least easy enough to complete quicker going straight through the main path, but for me - and I’m not a noob mind you since I have completed Dark Souls 1 and 3 and Sekiro, Elden Ring is simply too tough to my taste to call it enjoyable. As a side note, I might find the game so hard due to a faith build, meaning I use incantations in the game that are slow to cast in the heat of a battle, but this fact just tarnishes the game even more, because it truly doesn’t allow too much freedom in building the character if you want to excel as care free as possible - which you want, trust me. Now you might find this game fun and most players looking for combatting challenge will do at the beginning for a long while, but I label this review as negative due to the overall quality throughout the experience and the too cheap and frustrating challenge you will face eventually, no matter how good you are. If you are good, you will overcome the challenge, perhaps even quickly, but I doubt many of the fights are that fun in any case, unlike in Dark Souls 3 for example, where the game is thoroughly quite carefully designed, albeit unforgiving. Consider this game if you are ready to face this disappointment I’m feeling here and in the case you are a fan of the studio’s previous work, but for many, you should think twice, remembering that this game is far from GOTY material like some might claim, because the quality is so varying. I think sound design and graphics should be better as well to call this a GOTY, since the tech is like a mix of last-gen and current-gen, leaning more on the last-gen. Lastly about the mentioned technical side: The game runs decent enough if you have strong single core CPU performance and my RX 5700 XT plays it almost always at 60 FPS on max settings at 1440p, which the game is unfortunately capped at, but this hasn’t bothered me mentionably. There are areas that are bound to drop the framerate below 60 FPS, somewhere around 40 – 45, which is a slight annoyance, but those moments are rare. The game’s current version 1.08.1 is bug free, though it’s worth to mention that I experienced one freeze-up. Enjoy, suffer, be numbed, overcome, that is the formula of Elden Ring. Take this as you wish.

Like other FromSoftware games, the challenge of playing difficult bosses and beating them in and of itself is part of the rewarding experience. The scenery and some of the dungeons / locations can be stunning. My problem with this game is the open world aspect, the story lines, and the characters. The world is vast but empty. For the size of the world, NPCs are too few, most are simply silly and childish, and, like the bosses, they are unrelatable and there is no real depth to their story. What's more, your character, the overarching story line and the side quests utterly fail to captivate. Dungeons, mines, enemies, and boss fights are repeated over and over again in an attempt to populate the open world and weak story line. The endings are a total let down. This game is just too much of a waste of time for what one gets out of it.

After having played for over one hundred hours, I believe that this is my favorite game FromSoft has ever released. My first playthrough took sixty(!) whole hours to complete, so the game obviously has a plethora of content to enjoy. As with every other dark souls game, there is an immense amount of fun builds that you can choose from to suit every player's desired style. This make it all the more fun to challenge the game's difficulty. Difficulty in this game is set up in a way that makes it easier or harder depending on however the player decides to prepare themselves for something, due to the open world nature of Elden Ring. It's too hard. But quite possibly the best feeling responsive and fun mechanics of any game ive ever played. So just running around and dueling mobs is a top 10 gaming experience. But, If you dont consider yourself a hardcore gamer, with like 3+ months to invest into daily methodical grind, then dont expect to get far very soon. Maybe dont even try, I would honestly not recommend this game to your dad or your grandpa, or your friends that are not very in keen with gaming. You need to be a pretty good gamer to play this game. They really actually DO need to tone down on the difficulty just a smidgeon for it to be perfectly balanced. When people ask if its really that hard? yes, it is really that hard and harder than that when you actually jump in and see for yourself. But it is also very satisfying. You will play for a while, and think, oh this isnt that hard. Until it IS that hard. And you will understand the depth we speak about when reviewing this game. The map is massive. It is actually too big. There is never a point during the game where you actually have a good feel for where you are or where youre going. its just too much. Even when I have grinded this game out to absolute completion, the map still is too much for me to fully grasp at times. I remember thinking multiple times that I must be near completion of the game, and then realizing that I have only revealed maybe 10% of the game. And then after unvealing even further like 10x deeper than my original, I would start to think that the end must be in sight very soon. And yet, it wasnt. The end is so far beyond anything you could perceive, that you need to set aside all thoughts of ever finishing the game, and just hunker down and enjoy the process. Dont look for an end. Dont try to play it like you are trying to win right now. The game is just too long to think that way. Its ebven more massivbe than mmo's I have mastered in the past. I think there is a line in the sand when it comes to difficulty and progression. This is a balancing act where too hard and its a chore that isnt fun to do, too easy and you are bored. They nailed it, while at the same time, completely crossing way over that line and stressing the user out way beyond reason. And this title really does cross into that threshhold of being just a little bit way too much for reasonable gamers especially if you have any other commitments to attend to. I am a hardcore gamer, with titles to my name and a vast experience in pvp. It starts out and you basically just die, and die, and die. When You start to get a hang of it. The difficulty ramps up x10. And then the difficulty goes even further. You play for another 3 days nonstop, and then the difficulty progresses even further to a point that you couldnt even imagine when first getting through the initial skill cap. playing through this game reminds me, of like a journey through a difficult career. Where it never gets easier, it only ever gets harder the further you go, only, you become accustom to the increases of difficulty. You get used to the pain. You think the game will eventually even out and become fair as you level up and gain skill, but it never does. The ground you walk on, goes from being mountains and hills, to being on fire and ticking away your health. And it doesnt tick just a little bit of HP, it chunks out large portions of health non stop. And it isnt as simple as just use a potion. As some items are non recurring. Meaning you get a dead set # and you have to find these items. To turning into poison that kills you in 5 seconds, but you have to survive in it and fight some of the most difficult bosses and mobs for 3 hours somehow. The biomes continually get harder, in ways you wouldnt even expect. It's like the devs have an incredible talent for making punishing biomes for you to experience. If it ever gets too hot, maybe go back to that first biome where its all green bushes and grass. Because if you arent at least walking in fire and getting rolled up on by something that has an entire set of boss mechanics, consider yourself lucky because it will not last for long. What kept me going, is that the game is just so fun. I would not play for 2 days, and then I just NEEDED to play this game, because its just so, damn, fun. I couldnt stop. Even when I beat the game, I ended up doing 200 more boss run fights of just the same 1 boss I liked, just to figure out all the ways to perfect him so I could show off my skills in cooperative play. Even then, most boss fights, you can play 1000 times and still never get just perfect. You will still take a hit, or die in some unforseeable way. this very epic and hard boss. It only ever gets way harder to the point where you are finessing mobs with absolute skill and perfection, and yet you still die, reguardless of your perfect skills and mechanics mastery. The game is designed to be able to kill you even if you are playing perfectly. And at times you cant even believe that the game could get that much harder, but then it does, every step of the way, the levels get even more treacherous and difficult, and yet somehow, you will figure out a way through it. There are some fights you can get through 1 shot. There are some fights you can be clever and find a walk around or cheese method, or exploit. And then there are some fights where your currect charcter build demands that you just hunker down, and learn the fight absolutely perfectly, and then hope you get one lucky go. There are boss mechanics in the game, that actually really do cheat and dont make sense. You can play it perfectly and still get an unlucky go, and die. You will have to just die and die and die and maybe on the 10th or 15th time youll get through it. its a LOT of fun, but you need guts, and time, if you have the guts, go for it. There will probably never be another experience like it ever again. 10/10. Right now I probably would not play another game like this again, simply because its just too much most of the time, unless they made a game where you could actually stand a chance on your own without looking up guides. I had a constant 5 to 20 tabs open on my windows for guides for the vast amount of things this game has that you need to do or figure out. Its, a lot. It's literally actually too much. I would suggest they make the map like half the size next time also. And maybe not be such a complex maze even when you are standing in a grass and hill biome, its just too confusing and too easy to get lost. Like all you have to do is take a couple steps forward and you are lost and confused. look to the left, you are lost, look right, you are lost. That is one part they could improve in future designs. Take out a LOT of the complex hills and shrubbery, ect. Sometimes you just get tired of battling in a never ending maze, and especially when the maze is the size of the actual universe irl. with all this said, you cant play this game and not have fun. it's all about the mechanics, skills, spells, and weapons. they are just so good.

TLDR: Elden Ring, while imperfect, is the best implementation of an open-world action RPG that I've ever played. It feels like the culmination of every iteration of FromSoft's 'Souls' games into one truly amazing experience filled with intrigue, struggle, and eventual triumph. GENRE: Fantasy, third-person, open world, action RPG, 'Souls' game GAMEPLAY: Elden Ring is basically Dark Souls 4, or Dark Souls but now you can sneak, jump, and ride a steed around the open world areas. You start by creating a character and choosing a class to determine your starting gear and stats (e.g. Astrologer to be a spellcasting sorcerer, or Samurai to be a katana-weilding DEX melee build). You progress through the game by traveling around the map and finding items/gear to upgrade your equipment setup and defeating enemies to gain 'runes" that you can spend to level up or buy items from shops. 'Sites of grace' are the bonfire equivalents in Elden Ring, and most of the time they visually display a path of light that indicate the direction you need to head in to progress the main story through locations of major bosses. There are plenty of these grace sites littered everywhere in the open world and within dungeons so it is easy to fast travel to where you want to go immediately. Sites of grace' are the bonfire equivalents in Elden Ring, and most of the time they visually display a path of light that indicate the direction you need to head in to progress the main story through locations of major bosses. There are plenty of these grace sites littered everywhere in the open world and within dungeons so it is easy to fast travel to where you want to go immediately. Elden Ring is an open world game and there are various minidungeons/secrets hidden away in every corner of the map. It is to your advantage to seek out these locations to find rare materials and unique weaponry that may or may not change your play style altogether. The open world feels like there is always something waiting for you to discover, such as powerful enemies that drop unique weapon arts (ashes of war) or an NPC standing around waiting to offer you a quest. With the introduction of a day/night cycle, there are even some bosses that only spawn at nighttime in specific locations waiting to ambush you, but offer unique drops as well. GRAPHICS/PERFORMANCE: Elden Ring, at launch, was pretty shaky in terms of PC performance. I personally played this game to completion with below minimum specs. averaging 40-50 FPS at High settings. I encountered no game-breaking bugs/detrimental FPS hiccups in any playthrough, though the only issue I encountered was that enemies would sometimes become invisible on my screen whenever a large group of enemies were in an area, but they were still lock-on-able and would render again when I got closer/killed some of the group (this is probably just because my CPU is ancient). In terms of graphics, Elden Ring doesn't break new ground when it comes to overall presentation, but it is a very colorful game compared to previous Souls games. You can really tell when you enter a new region when all the colors transition from one palette to another and the sky/landscape dramatically changes as well. Dark areas are also pretty spooky as you can only see far enough from the light of your torch or lantern and enemies hide in the shadows very well. STORY: The long story short is: the Elden Ring was shattered into fragments and various demigods took the pieces to gain the fragmented powers within them. You are a 'Tarnished' which is basically a pseudo-undead human who is guided by grace to seek out the pieces of the Elden Ring, put them back together, and become Elden Lord in order to bring the world back to "order". (All of the details in between for NPC's and items is basically found in NPC dialogue and item descriptions for you to piece together, or until a genius puts all of the information together in a YouTube lore video) STRENGTHS: Combat feels the best it has ever been for 'Souls' games. Sneak attacks, jump attacks, ashes of war, NPC summons, mounted combat, guard counters, power-stancing, and everything else feels very, very good. Touching more on ashes of war, they basically allow you to add (and remove later) a unique skill to most non-unique weapons in the game. They also allow you to change the scaling of a weapon to a different one of your choice (if you also have the right whetstone) so you can make a weapon scale with INT or FTH even if it originally didn't. Boss encounters are exciting and challenging. If you feel underprepared, you can always to back to the open world and look for missed locations and items to better prepare yourself. (Also, feel free to use your ash summons whenever possible; it is a game mechanic after all) You can build a character however you desire, whether it be dual-weilding greatswords, holy knight, melee-spell-casting wizard, or pure archery. There are lots and lots of weapons to try, leading to more replayability as you try a new one in a future playthrough The crafting system is interesting as you can create consumables and throwable items when out of combat. You can even create bow/crossbow ammo which is very neat. Just when you think you're near the end, the map expands further and there is even more to discover. Compared to the other Dark Souls stories, Elden Ring's story feels the most digestible at face value without feeling completely puzzled from the outset. WEAKNESSES: PC performance isn't stellar if you are bothered by occasional FPS spikes or the rare game crash on loading screens. Not game-relevant, but the game doesn't fully "exit" when you quit out until a while later. Early game bosses reappear as 'mini-bosses' or just wandering around later game areas leading to some feelings of reused content. There is a massive spike in game difficulty from the mid-game to the late-game. It feels weirdly balanced when enemies all of a sudden go from doing 1/5 of your HP in damage to 1/2 of your HP in damage. UI could use a feature to compare stats of shop items with currently equipped items Online connectivity can be hit-or-miss. Sometimes when you are summoned to another world, you get a "connection error" and the game boots you back to single player. Be wary of hackers when playing co-op/PVP. Previous exploits have occurred where upon death, you would return to single player but be instantly dying forever because the hacker put you in an endless death loop. That exploit was patched, but we all know how hackers don't just give up. (Not a negative for me, but maybe if you like PvP): You can only invade other players if they are participating in co-op. Basically, unless a host uses a specific item, invasions usually lead to 1v2 or 1v3 scenarios (note: AFAIK fight clubs are only affected in that # of summonable participants is limited). I don't invade, but I've seen many people whining about this change when it makes sense why it is this way. So many important names sound very similar to each other that it could be difficult to remember who is who (e.g. Godwyn vs Godfrey vs Godrick). 'Great Runes' are pretty underwhelming in terms of power. Although I enjoy the game design of not having a dedicated questlog ingame, it is still to your benefit to just read an NPC's quest guide off the wiki to keep yourself on track. NUMERIC SCORE (if you care): 9.9/10; easy recommend Elden Ring has set my bar for 'open-world RPG' standards. The added gameplay features like jumping, horse-riding, sneaking, etc. make the game's action much more interesting and fun than previous FromSoft games. The game kicks my ass at every step of the way, but the struggle and eventual triumph is worth all of it. Though it is not without fault, I love this game and can't wait for future DLC.

After seeing probably around 98% of this games content throughout the course of over 130 hours on a single playthrough, Elden Ring easily makes for one of the greatest open world titles I've ever played. While I personally preferred the souls series' more linear style Elden Ring does do a great job at bringing the mechanics into an open world alongside so many small quality of life improvements that add up quite nicely. My main criticism would be that the overall quality of boss fights had some minor trade-off for more quality exploration but whether that counts as a net positive or negative is going to vary based on preferences. Mechanically it takes all the best parts of the Souls series and adds some great new elements, combat has so many more routes to find your preferred playstyle via Ashes of War, power-stancing, and mounted combat in many areas, new environments are incredible with particular note going to Caelid and the Haligtree as some of the coolest areas to come from a Fromsoft game, and of course practically bottomless rabbitholes for theorizing on lore. Absolute recommendation for anyone interested.

I have to first mention that i like to call myself a "souls-veteran". I have played every souls game except Demon s souls and completed them several times! Now onto the game itself, i have to say that since this is a souls game it is NOT for everyone, and you WILL die over and over and over until you finally beat that piece of s*** that killed you all those times (looking at you Malenia). That is the formula of these games, you die several times until you memorize the enemy s attacks and get a better chance at beating them. But i must also say that even though this is a souls game, in my personal opinion it is a good game for new players to the series, as you are not forced to fight everything you stumble upon. You can choose to fight that particular enemy over and over for several hours or you can decide to explore somewhere else, and come back later as this is the first time a souls game has gone full Open-World. In terms of gameplay there is a lot of different options for players, you can for example use a staff and deal magic damage from long range or choose to summon a FREAKING DRAGON HEAD to spew fire or frost or poison atyour enemies! You can choose to be a big burly warrior with a big a** sword, or you can choose to be more agile and dual wield katanas. Without spoiling anything too much for new players i have to say that the world is absolutely AMAZING, and the colors can range from pretty and green to red and downright terrifying. (people who has played the game know what i mean by RED and TERRIFYING). The only complains i have is that the endgame is BULLS*** as enemies deal WAY too much damage, and can also take quite a few hits even with the best weapons and equipment in your arsenal. And the game can stutter in some areas quite often. In summary, i think Elden Ring is a fantastic game from the genius mind of Hidetaka Miyusaki, and i reccomend people try this game! Do I recommend this game? If you like souls like games, then absolutely. If you’ve never played one I’ll still recommend it but keep some things in mind like making your decision to buy. It’s a souls like game so of course it’s incredibly difficult, but rewarding when you finally master combat and/or defeat an enemy. The graphics look great and the premise is solid. RPG style gameplay is so-so. You have no guidance, meaning there’s no quest markers. You run around the world finding dungeons and NPCs for quests and it’s not always clear what to do next. You don’t get a helping hand. This isn’t a negative per say, it just adds to the games challenge. A warning though, if you die, you drop your collected experience and must re-acquire it. If you die again before collecting it you lose it forever. It’s a great mechanic in my opinion, just a friendly warning. Combat is great most of the time but incredibly frustrating other times. Sometimes the controls are unresponsive or buggy. Enough so that if you’re an average skilled player you’ll lose your experience more to a bug than actually being bested by the games challenges. You’ll randomly stop blocking for a second, enough for a boss to get a clean hit in. Rolling/dodging is unresponsive sometimes. And because it’s a difficult game, a single mistake can mean defeat. I’d much rather lose to making the wrong decision, like dodging into an attack or mistiming a dodge. Mind you, I’m not referring to times when you get locked by animation, like healing or swinging your weapon. It’s when you’re standing still, and it won’t roll. Doesn’t make the game unplayable and it doesn’t happen often, but it makes the game far more frustrating that it needs to be. Getting bested is one thing, losing all of your experience because of a bug is another. Again, it’s not terrible, just an advanced warning to approach combat cautiously. Overall, I’ll recommend the game if you like a challenge. If you’re intrigued by the concept but are intimidated by the difficulty, you could try an easier souls like game like Jedi: Fallen order first. It’s pretty easy as far as souls style games go and doesn’t go into too much depth, but the combat is polished and rewarding.

Elden Ring leaves me conflicted, it is a good game, no doubt about it, definitely deserves GOTY. But the thing is, after playing the Dark Souls trilogy, it just doesn't hit the same. At the start of the game, it didn't really grab me and I didn't find it all that enticing. But once I reached the middle of the game, I got intrigued. Questlines like that of the volcano manor, were very well written and I found myself caring for a lot more NPC's in the game than in Dark Souls. Then the end, it was just underwhelming, after beating [spoiler] Malenia [/spoiler] and feeling one the greatest satisfactions I've felt, the end bosses were just a let down and the ending left me indifferent. [b]Furthermore:, some other smaller critiques I have:[/b] - Dual Boss fights, my god why so many. Slapping two enemies that are practically the same in one boss fight just doesn't work. - They really went all in on delayed attacks in this game my god, annoying! - Either the one of the hardest FromSoft games, or the easiest depending on what you limit yourself to. - Sometimes I felt overwhelmed by the intricacy of some areas like [spoiler]Stormveil Castle[/spoiler] or [spoiler]the capital[/spoiler] [b]The good:[/b] - Music 10/10 - Looks gorgeous - A lot more NPC's that actually matter and have an interesting questline. - Good sidequestlines! - The DS3 weapon art done right. - A lot more dynamics in your build through e.g MIxed Physicks, Rebirth and Ashes of War. - UI is defintely better than previous games. - The world is a lot more dynamic, espcially in dungeons were it sometimes felt like you were in liminal spaces. - The use of verticality in cities or castles in this game is amazing, the realization that I could just jump on a roof and explore an entire different part or route, took my breath away. Boy oh boy, this game is nothing less than great. Not only is this game cinematic the combat is fun the difficulty although at times can be a bit unfair is rather enjoyable, Being my first souls game I enjoy the experience a lot. Given that the game is cinematic which already makes an open-world game fun to explore, the music and looks tell you everything about the area. An example of this would be both the Leyndell Sewers and Caelid both of those areas feel uninviting as if you aren't supposed to be there. To be honest you probably aren't wanted there of the things that lurk in those places but that's what I love about the game the music, and the view all tell the same story of what's going on it, The game crafts and blends it all together beautifully. For the most part, all the bosses are fun, there are a couple of mini-bosses I dislike a lot and someone of them even required me to do some of those annoying ones for the completion of some character storylines, ( and a couple of boss fights that are required for the main story to progress that is horrible if you aren't prepared ). The game feels very rewarding for going out of your way to find things, and fighting the boss fights makes me feel like a badass when I finally manage to win. The story in Elden Ring also was amazing, a lot of people may say Elden Ring has no story, but that isn't the case it just has a different variation of storytelling. Such as Frenzy Flame (which the story starts at the very beginning of the game) or the story about the Lord of Blood (which is also something you'll likely run into). These little aspects affect the entire story and the more you learn about it the greater the connection grows with characters and the more it will hurt when some of said characters die. Elden Ring is truly a great game, regardless you mean the lore of a boss that you fought previously or a battle that you prepared for hours in advance. I personally felt a drive to win against those bosses as I imagined a world where they won and they succeeded. I would say this game is worth buying even at full price, but I wouldn't blame you for waiting for a sale.

This is honestly the worst Soulsborne game. The biggest problem is the bosses. If you play without spirits, you often have to dodge the boss for 20-30 seconds before you finally get an opportunity to get a hit in and go back to dodging for 30 seconds. The bosses lack a serious back and forth aspect, and that makes the fights very unsatisfying. This is without mentioning that bosses will randomly add attacks to the end of combo strings that seem "safe." Thus, the fight basically requires rote memorization through trial and error to understand which boss attacks are truly "safe" to respond to with an attack. If you play with spirits, the bosses become extremely easy and you essentially just abuse the enemy ai flaws. For a series known for its bosses, this game has very few fun boss fights. The next biggest problem is the open world. While the world is somewhat fun to explore in your first playthrough, the loot often feels spread way too thin compared to past games because unlike past soulsborne games, Elden Ring is an open world game. You often find crap that is irrelevant to your build waiting to find something that may finally get you to change weapons/armor/spells. And in the end, the open world. makes replays a complete slog. The best parts of the game end up being the legacy dungeons that aren't used enough. Overall, From Soft finally lost the ball on this one. I would not recommend the game over any other soulsborne game.

So many amazing things were achieved with Elden Ring, and although its undeniably a masterpiece and genius in terms of world building and design. There are significant issues that might ruin the game for a lot of the player base, especially on subsequent play-through's. With the exception of Godrick being a near perfect boss in terms of gameplay and design aesthetic. The boss quality of Elden Ring doesn't match up to their previous titles, Dark Souls 3 notably. Pretty much every main story boss in the game has at least one attack or more that is unreactable or purely unfair, with the end game bosses being the biggest offenders. But I will say that even though this may be an issue in terms of game design, Elden Ring is probably the easiest game Fromsoft has made given all the resources that are offered to you in game. Upon first play-through, someone might not have a problem running through the many side dungeons in the game because the act of finding a secret in the world adds spectacle, but this also has to do with the fact that most players wont know that the layouts and enemies used in these dungeons are reused over and over again, with little nuance. The side dungeons in Elden Ring are basically just the chalice dungeons from Bloodborne but worse; because Instead of getting something useful as a reward from a chalice dungeon like you would in Bloodborne, because of the extreme build diversity in Elden Ring, you are going to get something completely useless to your specific build ninety percent of the time. In addition to the side dungeons, certain bosses like the Ulcerated Tree Spirit are reused at least 10 times if you go through the trouble to find them all. Fromsoft has handled reusing bosses in the past very well but it isn't done well here. With all this in mind you might think that, "Well maybe you're only SUPPOSED to have one good play-through.". But this just isn't the case when you factor in the sheer number of different builds and weapons you can use and the fact it has a New Game + option. Considering the many flaws this game has, it doesn't stop this game from being one of the best games I have ever played. And without any of these flaws, Elden Ring would be undeniably one of the best games ever made. But it might still be up there even with its flaws. So maybe I just typed all of this out for zero reason. -20/10

Before Elden Ring, I had never played a From game before. But I was intrigued by all Elden Ring’s 10/10 ratings and the comparisons to Breath of the Wild, one of my favorite games. This is a review for people like me, who are intimidated by the reputation for difficulty but are still willing to consider it because of all those stellar ratings. OVERVIEW The plot, such as it is, is Lord of the Rings, except you want to seize the One Ring for yourself so you can conquer Middle-EarthTheLands Between. In typical video game fashion, the ring has been split into multiple pieces and you have to find and murder the owners of each piece. From a gameplay perspective, this means you explore ruins and dungeons, kill enemies, get better equipment and magic, level up, and repeat many times. There’s no other plot to speak of. NPC’s exist, but they mostly spout obscure and unintelligible gibberish. Developer From Software is infamous for offering only Hard Mode with no lower difficulty or accessibility options, and they did the same here. If you like to play on Story Mode, find Normal Mode in other games very challenging, or need accessibility settings beyond controller remapping, From Software doesn’t want your business and you can stop reading now. THE INTRO This is not a noob-friendly game, starting with character creation. You start with a class selector, with eight different class options. Each class has a bunch of numbers and symbols, but there’s no explanation of what any of those symbols mean or what abilities that class has. Then you pick a starting “boon”, from about fifteen options. What does this do? Is it important? Also no explanation. The combat tutorial is a brazen “fuck you” to noobs, because they stick it off the side where you can easily just walk right past it, and even when you go through it it barely explains how any of the systems work. After the tutorial, same story. As you gain power, you pick stats to level up and pick weapons and equipment. When you do this, Elden Ring’s developers give you a stats screen full of tiny, barely-legible numbers. Fortunately, my husband is a Dark Souls fan who had already played the game. He helped me pick a class, pointed out the tutorial that I wandered past, explained how blocking works, pointed out more stuff when it was clear I didn’t understand some system, and gave me pointers on how to pick stats to level up. Having someone to help was absolutely essential. Without my husband’s advice, I would have given up in frustration within the first two hours. THE GOOD PARTS. THEY’RE REALLY GOOD Once past that initial hurdle, things got a lot better. The world design is S-tier. You walk (or ride) around, and look at the environment, and you can be sure that no matter which direction you go you will find something. Quest markers and checklists are nonexistent. Points of interest are common and clearly telegraphed, while the path to get there is not always obvious, so you have to look around and figure out what to do. No matter what the point of interest is, what you find there will almost always be combat. Combat being the only objective sounds like it would be repetitive, but it isn’t. By varying the size and shape of battle arenas and the types of enemy groupings, Elden Ring makes encounters become completely different even when facing enemies you’ve seen many times before. Elden Ring keeps this variety up for the whole game, which is truly remarkable for how big it is. Unfortunately, the game doesn’t have much to find that’s not combat. You’d expect that in a hundred-hour game they would liven things up a bit, but there are no towns, no puzzle shrines, no suspiciously placed rocks that hide collectibles, few platforming challenges, and no hidden paths to jawdropping views. Even so, the content that does exist is pretty great. BUT IS IT TOO HARD? Well, no and yes. And ultimately, yes. It took a few hours to get the basics down, including some advice from my husband. After that, I would characterize it as “challenging but fair”. Even regular mobs deal a lot of damage and you have a very limited supply of healing potions. Traps and ambushes are common. But it will normally not take you more than a few tries to take out a group of regular enemies, and if it’s too hard you can just move on and come back to slaughter them later. At least for a while. The bosses are a different story. The boss difficulty is not reliably matched to the difficulty of the dungeon it’s in. Sometimes the bosses are easily dispatched, but often they are absurdly, unfairly difficult. The game seems to be expecting you to try bosses dozens of times before you win. Many games have implemented this sort of challenge design well, but Elden Ring isn’t one of them. Instead of instantly respawning you near where you failed, the game routinely sticks respawn points several rooms away from the boss chamber, the battles are long with no mid-battle checkpoints, and the death animations and load times are glacial. I started timing one these battles, and found that for every twenty seconds of fighting the boss, I spent twenty-eight seconds on death animations and loading screens, and another fifty on walking from the respawn point back to the boss chamber. What a waste of time. Eventually, I gave up on even trying to fight the bosses. Instead, I would clear the rest of the dungeon, unlock the boss chamber, and come back fifteen or twenty hours later to fight the boss. Occasionally, this resulted in a truly epic battle where I survived with a sliver of health. Sometimes, it was a tough but fair challenge. But it most often resulted in a pushover. Then I got near the endgame (I think), and the game collapsed. I had done every bit of content I could find, and no matter where I went everything was too hard. The five headed dragon guarding the fourth shard? The remaining optional overworld bosses I had skipped?. The optional minidungeon I had skipped? The next legacy dungeon blocking the critical path? Everything was too hard, in every direction. That was when I gave up, over a hundred hours in. I probably *could* have cleared it by playing the game’s way, trying each challenge dozens of times, spending the majority of my playtime on loading screens and walking from respawn points to bosses and tough enemies. Or I could have embraced the fact that this is technically a JRPG and ground mobs for hours until I got another twenty levels. But why? That’s not fun. BUY OR NO BUY? Overall, Elden Ring was a bizarre mix of really spectacular top-tier content and frustrating bullshit. This world design is everything I’ve wanted from an open world, so much better than other titles, and the combat is often fair and well-designed. But the hostility to players who don’t already understand the systems and a terribly implemented “try over and over until you get it right” approach to boss design are really bad. So should you play it? Well, if you can mitigate the atrocious load times because you have a current-gen console or high-specs PC. Statistically, you probably don’t, but maybe you do. Elden Ring is one of, if not the most overrated and overhyped games I have ever played. This isn't a "skill issue" and I don't need to "get good". Pinning blame on the players is a way that I've seen Elden Ring fanboys obfuscate from actual problems the game has. Compared to nearly every other From Software game except maybe Demons Souls or Dark Souls 2, Elden Ring is outshone in nearly every conceivable way. The combat is just unsatisfying, the npcs are some of the worst in the series, and the open world aspect just does not work in the context of a souls-like game. The visual design in this game in general, except for maybe a few specific examples, is just unappealing in a way that makes areas not as interesting as previous games. Elden Ring has inconsistent design philosophies which makes the game feel unnecessarily frustrating at times. The game is filled with gank fights and unnecessary annoyances. A distant ledge that looks to be part of a wall could lead to a secret or may be blocked by an invisible wall that causes you to fall to your death. The game feels like it was made by people who had no communication with each other. The game also suffers from copy and paste, cookie cutter, pre-fabbed dungeons which comprise of nearly all of the games side content. In these dungeons you may find an interesting boss, but it most certainly also appears in at least 3 other dungeons and the reward will likely be not worth the effort you put into the dungeon. All of this could be excused, and I could accept this game as just being a subpar slip into From's library, if not for the atrocious optimization that still hasn't been fixed over a year after release. It is honestly some of the worst I have seen coming from a triple A studio in recent years. If anyone tells you that Elden Ring is their favorite soulsbourne game, either they haven't played many soulsbourne games, or they've seen something in the game that I just haven't. If you are looking to see if this game is worth buying or not, save yourself $20 and buy Dark Souls Remastered instead.
